THE FREE CHURCHES.
THE CONGREGATIONAL 17NION.

The meetings of the Congregational Union at Newcastle have been a great success. The achievements of Mr. Carvell Williams and Dr. Guinness Rogers made the Congregationalists prouder than ever of their cider men. Dr. Rogers looks younger every day, and by retir- ing from his pastorate he seems to have renewed his lease of life. Among the younger men the Rev. J. H. Jowett, of Birmingham, perhaps made the most impression. Mr. Jowett is now among the half-dozen greatest Free Church preachers in England. Ho has con- fessed that he has a passion for preaching. Even when he comes on to a platform to make a speech, it is only a sermon in disguise.

div.head: POPE AND TEMPORAL POWER..
div.p: THE POPE AND TEMPORAL POWER..

Dr. Horton contributes a rather strikins article to the November Free Churehnuzn on "A Holiday in Italy." He narrates that he was travelling to Siena with a young Italian pet who was closely related to the Pope's Chamberlain. "I asked him whether there was any pcssibility of the restoration of the tem- poral po Ker. He turned to the first person who was at hand, the man, by chance, sitting next to him in the carriage, and put the question to him. The reply was an immediate and deci- sive and almost impatient No.' The Vatican ia moving, I will not say Heaven, but earth; it is laying a hand on Germany, America, and England to recover that Sovereignty over the Kings of the earth, which was built up in tho Middle Ages. If it succeeded, the modern world would, like the mediceval world, be brought to a dying pass. In the attempt Italy, the mother country of the Roman Church, is torß asunder and brought to the verge of ruin. But success is impossible."

div.head: NONCONFORMISTS IN THE NEW PARLIAMENT
div.p: NONCONFORMISTS IN THE NEW PARLIAMENT

Mr. R. W. Perks, M.P., who is being looked upon more and more as the Nonconfor- mist leader in the House of Commons, says that Nonconformity will be stronger than ever in the new Parliament. The Christian World has published a list of Non- conformist M.P.'s Twenty-five of them are Congregationalists, four Baptists, thirty-three Methodists, thirty-five Presbyterians, and three members of the Society of Friends. Great regret is felt at Mr. Albert Spicer's defeat in the Monmouth boroughs. A new Noncon formist member, of whom great things are expected, is Mr. Alderman George White, of Norwich. Mr. White has taken a keen interest in the Free Church Fed eration Movement and

is President of the East Norfolk Federation He is an impressive speaker—calm, clear, and logical. He has the temperance and edu- cation questions at his finger ends, and will not he afraid to stand up, even to Mr. Chamber- lain.

div.head: Ant. PRICE HUGHES AND MARIE CORELLI.
div.p: Ant. PRICE HUGHES AND MARIE CORELLI.

Mr. Price Hughes has been lecturing at St. James's Hall, London on "The Master Christian." It is difficult to make out exactly what Mr. Hughes thinks of the book, but he bows with respect to an author who can secure 1)0,000 readers bef ore her work has over seen the light. Whoever can get a large audience, .11 Mr. Hu ghee opinion, must have something to say well worth hearing. Mr. Hughes de- nounced Miss Corelli's attack on the Wesleyan ministers as stupid, vulgar and false. He praised the courage which she showed in dealing with religious problems.

div.head: SUMITLTANEOITS MISSION.
div.p: THE SUMITLTANEOITS MISSION.

The interest in the Simultaneous Mission increases as the preparations go forward. Even the most sanguine leaders of the movement have been astounded at the eagerness and en- thusiasm with which local Councils throughout the country are taking up the matter. There is every prospect that, the gigantic project Of the originators will be carried out, in its entirety. The Press has been rendering the movement very valuable help. Long articles on the mission have appeared in the British Weekly, Christian World, the Puritan, the Quiver, Daily News, the Manchester Guardian, Nottingham Daily Express, Western Mercury, Sheffield Independent, und many other journals and magazines. The earnestness with which the project is being taken up shows that it has seized the imagina- tion and caught the enthusiasm of Free Church- men everywhere. Free 'Church Councils throughout the country are devoting all their energy towards making it a success. All the other items of their programme are taking a übordinate place.

div.head: FREE CHtIRCH MISSION WORK.
div.p: FREE CHtIRCH MISSION WORK.

In the meantime the missions conducted by Gipsy Smith and Mr. W. R. Lane, the mis- sioners of the National Council, are enjoying remarkable success. At Bath, three thou- sand tickets for Mr. Smith's leettire on his life could easily have been sold if there had been room for the people. Indeed, one of the vendors of the tickets had to refuse applications for five hundred in one morning, and many of those who came offered him half- a-crown or more for a ticket. The Gipsy has also conducted missions with great success at Croydon and Dulwich. Mr.W. R. Lane's work at Newbury also made a deep impression. The Corn Exchange, providing accommodation for 1300 people, was filled every night. Mr. Lane has no eccentricities or tricks of oratory, but holds his audience by sheer fore. of honest, manly, believing speech. There is no affectation, no mere pietism, no overstrained emotion. He speaks as to reasonable men, and above all, as to men with a conscience.

div.head: FREE CHURCHES AND WORKING-MEN.
div.p: THE FREE CHURCHES AND WORKING-MEN.

The Rev. F. B. Meyer, 8.A., greatly deplores, like all thoughtful Christians, the alienation from the Church of Christ of large masses of hard-headed working-men. He suggests that the Free Church Councils through the country should invite the representative working-men a their localities to meet them in conference, to consider how far we are responsible, by mistakes that we might remedy, for the present state of things. "Of course, where it is due to the antipathy of the human heart to the Gospel, we cannot make concessions or lower our standard. But it may be that there are stones of misunderstanding and groundless suspicion that we might roll away from betweefr the dead and the voice of Christ."
THE MOST NUTRITIOUS.

BREAKFAST AND SUPPER.
LADIES' LETTER.
MY DEAR NELLIE,

Where the facial angle of the face is a very long one from the crown of the head to the chin the toque should fit well down upon the head towards the cars, instead of being lifted away from them, as in the boat-shaped hat. A toque, becoming to almost any face, is made ef black velvet and trimmed with feathers and a knot of brightly. tinted silk or ribbon. There is no exaggeration about any of these hats. Some are wearing monstrously large headgear. Chinchilla and painted panne compose many of the new hats, the brim being in the fur, the full crown in the panne. Buckles are still indispensable to smart headgear. Folded panne is a beautiful material to choose for an autumn toque, and makes even the most cleverly manipulated cloths look clumsy. It shines like satin, and is not as heavy as velvet. The blue tulle rosettes Set on high on many hats have a couple of painted panne quills tucked through them.

A black silk or satin blouse, plainly made, either tucked or herring-boned, slightly pouched over a handsome waistbelt, is a useful item of the winter wardrobe, and it always looks well with any skirt if the coat is removed or thrown open. A cream satin ditto is also useful for smart occasions, especially for luncheon parties, when the coat is sure to be taken off, and the neck can be finished off with good lace. A typo of skirt useful to wear with a silk shirt is the corselet skirt, the top part being shaped like a Swiss belt with a peak uprising back and front, under which the shirt is tucked, keeping all neat without a waistbeltt Many pretty blouses are made of strips of ribbon united together by an openwork crochet work known as the hairpin stitch. The blouse is made up quite plainly over a coloured lining' and fastens at the side. The same treatment is also applied to silk or satin skirts.

The reign of the velvet dress has set in agata ; for long it has been banished from our midst, at all events for street wear, now it is once more with us, in black chiefly, sometimes plain, sometimes with its surface covered with spots of various dimensions.

Furs are now employed on outdoor and indoor and evening gowns to an enormous extent. Whole sables form the brims of hats and toques, and the whole skin is often arranged on jackets as a sort of revers, coming from the right shoulder to the waist. It is noticeable that the high, upstanding collar is seldom visible on good models; all turn down closely round the throat, or extend on to the shoulders like a small cape. Black velvet, too, makes some of the modish three-quarter length loose coats, trimmed with rich furs, and here be it said that furs are the fittest trimming for black velvet. The passementerie of jet and the bugles which are so often seen give it the touch of vulgar commonplaceness which has caused it to fall rather into disrepute.

A goodly portion oi the fashionable skirt rests on the floor, spreading out like a fan about the wearer. Some of the new dresses are made with sheath-like straightness as far as the knee, whence they flow out with rather an abrupt change of line, which is inartistic. Some are pleated perpendicu- larly to the same point, and pleated or stitched horizontally below it. A skirt may be cut all in one, and yet given the effect of being double by this means, so great is the apparent increase of width produced by the contrast between down- ward lines and those running round the figure. As to bodices, they are very much trimmed, especially in front, whore the line of the figure is very often broken up by means of revers, boldro or zouave. Sometimes the fronts fall sheer from the shoulders to a couple of inches below the waist; but this has the result of making the body from the waist downwards look very short. Your bring_

div.head: (Copyright.)
div.p: (Copyright.)
THE HOUSE BY THE RIVER.
BY MRS. C. N. WILLIAMSON, author of "The Secret. of the Pearls," "The House by the Lock," "Queen Sweetheart," "The Barnstormers," "Her Royal Highness," tto.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: Lancelot Wade, a well-connected ne'er-do-well, lives with his daughter Sybil in fourth-floor rooms in Blooms- bury. One day the father brings Sybil the extraor- dinary news that she—she who never went anywhere or saw anybody in her life—is to go to a dinner- party at Lady Northmuir's house in Berkeley-square, where she meets a certain Jack Churchill, who is expected by Lady Carstairs, another guest, to marry her daughter Gladys. The dinner, like the house, is very grand, and Sybil is supremely uncomfortable. Next mornine Lancelot Wade does not appear at breakfast; Sybil finds that his bed has not been slept in. Alarmed, she is about to go to the police- station, when a messenger-boy appears with a letter from her father. The envelope is blood-smeared, and the messenger hesitatingly admits that he thinks there has bem an accident. Sybil is conducted by the messenel r-boy. by means of trams and trains, quite out of the city to a lonely house on the river bank. She is told to enter a certain room, and, expecting to see her father, she unhesitatingly enters. The nom is empty! And Sybil, when she tries to get out again,finds herself a prisoner. Mean- while Churchill, on his way to the birthday-feast of Gladys, reads of Lancelot Wade's suicide, and carries tne news to Lady Carstairs. At the close of the last cha iter they are discussing Sybil Wade's VAture. Churchill does not know that Sybil has dis- appeared. and Lady Carstairs seeks to quench his interest in her by lying to him about the way she is being cared for and the low marriage she is about to contract. Lady Carstairs herself at this time does not know what has become of Sybil and she seeks the assistance of her son, Lord Carstairs, to get her put out of the way so that Churchill shall never sea her and discover the lies told about her. It is very evident that Lord Carstairs has a powerful private motive for getting rid of Sybil, though his mother knows nothing of it as yet.
CHAPTER IX. LORD CARSTAIRS ASTONISHES HIS FRIENDS.

As Lady Carstairs talked on, the strange signs of axeitement in her son's dark face were gradually controlled. He walked up and down, listening, even smiling an odd, cynical smile from time to time, as she dilated upon the tactics to which she had had occasion to resort.

"So you told Churchill you would let him know something more about the girl to-morrow, after you had been to call on her, did you ?" he inquired at last, with quiet grimness. "Yes," she rejoined. "And I really mean to go. I shall drive down to Mitchell-street directly after breakfast."
"I wouldn't, if I were you, mater." " Why not ?" "Because your beloved little niece is no longer there."

Lady Carsta:rs's eyes opened. "No longer there? Then you know—you have ready— The young man did not meet his mother's eager glance as he replied. "Naturally. I had to make arrangements about that unfortunate beggar, Lancelot Wade, you know; and—er—l thought someone would have to break it to the girl ; so that, if she'd been fussing about him since his disappearance, the news of what he had done to himself mightn't come to her through the newspapers." "I'm sure that was exceedingly good of you, my dear boy!" said Lady Carstairs, genuinely astonished. "Is it possible that her apparently extraordinary fascinations—l confess I couldn't see them—appealed powerfully to you, as well as Mr. Churchill, on that eventful evening when the girl and her father (lined here, or—" Carstairs shrugged his shoulders. "You must think what you choose," he answered. "I only stipulate that, if lam to help you and Gladys to what you want, you must v.sk me no questions whatever—" "You do mean to help us, then ?" Gladys exclaimed, breaking into the conversation for the first time. She had never, in all her experience of him, known her brother to be so amenable. "I do mean to help you—under those conditions," he echoed. "But, look here, muter, you are to tell Churchill to-morrow that Sybil Wade is more prostrated by the shock of her father's death than she realised at first. You are sending her into the country directly the funeral is over for a complete change; the doctor you intend to see about her may recommend a nursing home. And she is to have every attention and comfort. Can you remember all that? "

"Perfectly!" Lady Carstairs thoughtfully returned. Her curiosity was greatly excited. Was all this mere invention on Carstairs s part? And, if so, why should he be suddenly ready, for once in his life, to put himself to trouble for his mother and sister ? . _ _ _
"Will the girl really be quite safely kept out of Jack Churchill's way for ever ? " she could not help asking, though questions were forbidden. "Quite safely," Carstairs echoed—"for ever
p---- CHAPTER X. A CORNER UNDER TIIE EAVES.

The suspense had grown intolerable to Sybil Wade in the long hours she had spent in the locked room of that old house by the riverside. Twilight Lad closed in, night had fallen, and no one had come to release her. Yet now she grew gradually certain that the sound she heard was not due to rats in the wainscot, but to the stealthy footsteps of someone or something in the room. Faint and weary as she was, the girl had become well-nigh incapable at last of vivid terror or ,intense emotion of any kind. She was afraid; but with a cold creeping fear that was almost apathetic. She could not move. The sounds, so slight in them- selves, drummed in her ears, and were curiously exaggerated to a noise as loud as the crackling of dead' leaves in an autumn wind. "Hist !" sharply whispered a voice. "Are yon awake or asleep? " Sybil recognised the tones of the messenger who had brought her to the house, and her heart beat more naturally. "I'm awake," she answered._ - . - -

_ "Rush ! Don't speak so loud !" warned tho voice in the darkness. It was close to her now— so close that she could feel a warm breath across her cheek. Then a groping hand touched her hair, gliding down over her shoulders till it had grasped her arm. "If anyone hears us talking together, the game's up. I can't do anything more." "What game ?" asked Sybil, whispering also now. "The game of—of serving you if I can. It will be hard work, and two chances to one against success at best. But don't ask any questions, it's only a waste- of time, for I can't and won't answer if you do. Give me your hand if you mean to trust me, and we'll go out by the way I came. I daren't light a match." The fingers clasping Sybil's arm found her hand. They were small--almost as small as her own—and icy cold. Sybil shivered, and half drew back as the other would have pulled her along through the darkness. "Why should I trust you?" she protested. "You told me what was untrue when you told me Ton were taking me to my father. You must have known what would happen, for you are no real messenger-boy. You are acquainted with the people in this house, and " The hand fell away from Sybil's, and left her standing alone in the blackness which her eyes could not penetrate, strain as they would. "Very well," whispered the voice. "If you won't trust me, I can't say anything that will make you. I've done my best to help you ; but I can't force you to come with me against your will. I'll have to go away and leave you to—to the things that I wanted to save you from, for I can't stay here. lit tell you just this—it's as much as my life is worth to have come at all, and you must decide what you're going to do in two minutes." "What will happen to me if I stay ?" Sybil questioned, fearfully. "Do you know that, or----" "Yes ; I know, or I wouldn't be here now," tho other broke in quiclly. "You will die." "You mean that someone will--"

Sybil's voice faltered. She could not utter the dreadful words that had sprung into her mind. "The two minutes are up," _whispered the messenger. "Am I to go without you?" "No!" exclaimed Sybil." Don't leave me! I will trust you! Something seems to tell me that you won't deceive me again." Instantly she felt her hand clasped once more, and a slow groping progress along the wall began. Sybil supposed that the door must have been upened while she slept, and closed again, though perhaps not locked; but presently, as she followed the guidance of her unseen companion.
ouchlng suen objects as she passea on the Way, she felt the door. paused, and found that she was being led further on.

"How are we to get out.?" she ventured to whisper. "We have just gone past the door." "Wait!" whispered the other. "Oh, here we arc at he place! Bend down your head veil- low —as low as you can—and come after me. I won't let go your hand." Sybil's guide, instead of proceeding straight on, turned abruptly to the left. The girl stooped, according to instructions, groping with her free hand, and discovered that she stood in front of a low narrow opening in the wainscot. Scarcely had she passed through, when her companion stopped; there came the sound of a panel cautiously pushed along a groove, with a faint clicking noise at the end. Sybil felt a slight tug, as if someone had dragged at her gown, and discovered that it had been shut in with the closing of the door. She tore at the skirt to pull it free, while her guide exhorted her in whispers to make haste. The stuff yielded, and she hurried on, still in the dark, not conscious that a tell-tale shred of serge had been left behind.

It seemed to her that they went down a short passage, so narrow that her slim shoulders touched the wall on either side, and then there cline again the -sliding of wood along a groove. Sybil came near stumbling over a couple of shallow steps that led up to a doorway, as low or lower than the other, and beyond felt that she stood in a wider space. The hand that had held hers was withdrawn, and a second later came the scratching of a match. A little yellow flame leaped up, shelving the face of the messenger-boy, but a person so different from the smart little figure in uniform she had seen in the afternoon that involuntarily Sybil uttered a cry of astonishment. "Hush, hush! for Heaven's- sake !" came a viaming whisper, as the figure moved across a r)om, dimly seen by the light of the match, and touched the flame to a candle on a high mantel- piece. "Why, you—you are not the messenger-boy, after all!" exclaimed Sybil. "You look exactly like him, yet—yet you are a woman! Are you his sister?"

"His sister!" The girl laughed bitterly beneath her breath. "Can't you guess that we are even more nearly related than brother and sister? But there's not time to discuss that now. Whoever I am, you must take me on faith. And let me tell you that if you and I were in prison, sentenced to be hanged to-morrow morning, we shouldn't be in much greater danger of death than we are now. So speak softly; don't ask questions about unneces- sary things, and listen to everything I say." Sybil did not speak. She was waiting for what should come next. Even now she could not rid herself of the sensation that she was living and moving in a dream. Her eyes wandered about the room. It, like the other in which she had passed so many anxious hours was wainscotted, and furnished in a solid, old-fashioned way. There was a door, but Sybil could not see the low entrance by which she and her companion had come in. The other girl pointed meaningly. to the floor.

"Downstaii-s," he whispered-L4 in a room that lies beneath this one and the other I have just brought you out of—two people are sitting. I listened to what they were saying, and, though I couldn't hear much, I know that they ate talking of you, and how to put you out of the way. At any moment they may come up and go to that other room. If they do that before we are gone, we are both as good as dead; they would have no more mercy on me than on you, because I have betrayed them, and they would think that I might do so again if they let me live. But I had to bring you here, or leave you where you were, for I haven't the key of the other room. I don't think they know of the panels that slide back, and the passage between the rooms; for if they did they would not have had you put there. Now you see why I whisper, and why I tell you to do the same, if you care for your life—and mine. If they hear my footsteps overhead, it does not matter, for this is my room. I live in this house. But if they fancied they heard other footsteps, too, they would suspect something wrong, and come Itp."

By the death of Prince Christian Victor. at Pretoria, to which the Queen made a touching reference, in her message of welcome to the City Imperial Volunteers, Her Majesty loses yet another grandson, and much sympathy is felt for our aged Sovereign. for Priece and Princess Christian, and their family. The Princess was on the point of having Windsor for London, to take part in the C.I.V. celebrations, when she received tee sad intelligence that her e'der and much-leved 6011 had passed away—a victim to that terribly fatal disease which has killed such vast numbers of our soldiers. A more united family than that of Cumberland Lodge, it would be impossible to imagine, and this blow is indeed a crushing one, to the hitherto happy little circle. Prince Christian Victor had all his mother's grach us charm of manner,and possessed not one scrap of " side" —ln fact, if there was one thing he disliked more than another, it was to be reminded of his Royal rank, much preferring to be addressed as a simple English gentle- man—Apropos of this, a story is told to the effect that when Mr. F Villiers, the well-known war correspondent was delivering an interesting and amusing lecture at Wellington, on tbe famous battle of Omdurman, Mr. Villiers observed the Prince (who had just returned from Egypt, where he :acquitted himself most creditably) sitting in the front. It was somewhat natural that in the ccurse of his lecture, he should introduce tulegy— in no wise exaggerated—on the bravery of the Prinoe. As might have been expected this eve ked a burst of cheering from the toys assembled. The Prince,however, was anything but gratified at this, and left soon after- wards, remarking to a master, that lie had come down with several others, as an" old boy " and wished to b 3 ' received as such. Cumberland Lode, which is situated in the midst of Windsor Great Park, although a Royal residence can scsrcely be termed a stately English home. It is just I a plcturesque, old-world looking mansion, whose ivy- clad walls convey a sense of internal comfort. rattier I than of state, which is confirmed as one passes the threshold, and notes the home-like cosy air, which per- vades every apartment. It was hero that Priceess. Christian had the news broken to her of the death of her son. Only Princess eisbert of Anh tit, her younger dauebter, was her, Prince Cnristian being in Ger- many ; Princess Victoria with the Queen at Balmoral ; and Prince Albert with his regiment, the Hessian Guard Dragoons. It seems impossible to believe, when looking at Lady I Grosvenor, that she can possibly be a grandmother—yet I the fact remain., the infant son of Lady Shaftesbury I , having bestow( d the title upon her—Lady Grosvenor, still a very handsome woman, was one of the beauties of her day, and her daughters, Lady Shaftesbury. and Lady Lettice Grosvenor, are both exceedingly beautiful women, possessing moreover in a large aegree, their motber'a sweetness of disposition, and happy sunny temperament. Lady Grosvenor is eagerly looking foe- ward to the return of her son, the Duke of Westminster., from South Africa, when great rejricings, at Eaton Hall, , will be the order of the day. Women are becoming as active in the field as in other spheres of lifeeind the names of no fewer than five ladies appear among the" masters "of hounds for the coming season. The athleticisna of women has been,in faclein Mr' Gladstone's appropriate phrase, advancing by leaps and bounds, and eniy quite recently a well known girls' school n-ar London appointed a professional cricket instructor. Women are also forming their own clubs, for the various kinds of sport, such as swimming, skating, , hockey, and so on. Of still greater importance is the Ladies' Golf Union, which has been instrumental in organising women's golf clubs, and only lately it has I ventured to question the authority of the Royal an] Accieet Golf Club, of St. Andrews,as governing the laws of the game. The National Union of W men Workers, which ha; been holding its meetings at Brighton, largely owes its origin to Miss Ellice Hopkins. She began organising women's meetings in 1878, and the first ef the annual Conferences was held at Barnsley in 1889. Since then similar gatherings have been held at Nottingham, Gies- pow, Manchester, Leeds, Liverpool, and this year at Brighton. Some critics say that the woman's pl.ce in at home, and that these public discussions do not lead to any practical good' That is far from being the case, and it is to these discussions that we have to look for uetful thoughts, and to endeay.ur to turn them into moroments for the b:nefit of society. As to the CC plaint that croa.en do not conc•An thanselv,:s enough with the business of the household, it is not generally true. It would be more correct to say that the great majority of wernen overwork themselves, and far more willingly than their husbands, surrender every scrap of their leisare to the interests of the home. On the subject of education, Mrs Bryant said, at the Brighton Conference, that whilst the girls of the poorer families were excellently taught, those of the mi Idle and upper classes were often indifferently educated. The reascn for this is not far to seek. I- arises from the I superiority of the Beard Soho ds over the inefficient governess and private school favoured by the will to do classes. It is true there has been a eeneral levelling up of girls' schools, in recent years, but many, whilst mak- ing great pretensions, are really very backward. To no small extent, the improvement, where it has been (if cted, is due to throwing open Gov rernent offices to our sex, but in these days,when almo-t every profession is open to we men, there are few, who are in any sense competent, who care to accept the position of a governess. With regard to the d;fireulty of aleteining domestic ! servants, many suggestion., more or less practicable I were made' One idea was that meals should be cooked I outside the house, and brought round in hot water 'carriers. Many people have thought of this before, and ! have wendered why some enterprising tradesmen have I not tried the plan of supp ying the public with hoe din- ners at their own homes. Something ot the kind will no doubt be tried sooner or later, and it is prohable that ter. , business will yield satisfactory returns. Another vlew was, that the servants should lice nutside, end only come in by the day or hour, each one being r, six cail,se This is pretty much the 55 stem adopted in India, and I the proposal suggests the iriquire why, if we are to I adopt the Indian methods we should not &leo employ I Indian servant,. Whatever suggestions may be made, it seems to be more than 1 kely that the servant question Will become every year more acute, and that heusewi V.q , will either have to do the work themselves, or go to ! other countries for assistance. The mitten is in great request again just now, amone ue- iate-women, the rewest I:ing fashioned out of real , lace, with a point coming well over the knuekas. TnP idea is quaint, and of clurs admits of a display of handsome rices,but otherwise it has litt'e to rt c mmend it. A nice, well-fitting glove, is really more desirelele .from every noint oi view. The " cuff " bouquet seems to have cilia] " e.sueht on," and without doubt it possesses et taiderahle ad- vantages. Built en a stiff cut!, covered with ribbee te match the flowers used, it has a " sho weft" offs et, a big bow of the ribbon anteesrieg in the midst of the trailing bloomS. Nombers of women are donning the " cuff" bougoet, which is invariably worrs nn the left wrist, 5. day as %eel as nieht. the mode dcitil away with all damage invsriab:y dens', when flowers are pinned to the enrsasse. It is indeed a meter for regret that white, and lieht colcured fa brine are to be tabnoed by Dime Fashion this winter. Thanks to the marvels of dry rltanin.r, we cm get these hack over and over again, practically as go d as new, which convinces one that lieht cslourel ger- merits are quite as economical as ea k ones. Cream homespun. co take one trample. from the sturdieess t its Scotch and Irish make, will canoe hick funs the cleaners looking atialuttly na,-r, over arid over iseain. div.head: RURAL LABOURERS
div.p: RURAL LABOURERS

P 'or serfs, to !Amu only born, ' l'is our. t ) rise with early morn. The dar's long round of toil Co mint And only when the night is nigh, And stars bnia to dot the sky. We homeward turn our weary feet. Bat far from cities, and thrir ways. We pass our peaceful nights and d whr.re Nature sweetens cur employ ; Our East( lies in the rural seen.. Where fi Ms are fair, and meadows greAo, And dear the woodland songs of joy. And surely 'rrath Gals lovely sun, No nooler work than ours is done, lives more useful ever led . We till the ground that crops may come, Ar.cl bar the precious harvest .home, That still supplbs the world. with bread. Yet in this land 80 rich, so free, What poll., whit landless sous are we. Without a cot, a barn, or snore; Wit we may toil and try to live Upon the doles our masters give. And die when we can toil no more.

But, patient still, we murmur not, B,nce God himself rogards our lot, And 1114 own ways aro always best ; Thro,lgh Ll:m our life of toil so hard, Will surely meet a bright reward LI one of everlasting rest. J. H. W. CLINDINNING.

div.head: I "Let us-hurry away,'-then)''' begged Sybil:
div.p: I "Let us-hurry away,'-then)''' begged Sybil:

"That is whit I wistit to do; b I liad to mare you understand the risk first. And it maybe, too, that when we go into the passage outside this door —as we must to leave the room—we may meet them face to face. But I'll go first and see if the coast is clear; after that we must take our chances."

I The girl's dark face was deadly pale in the wavering light of the candle, and the look in her great eyes made Sybil's heart beat quickly. There was no thought of distrust lurking in Sybil's mind now; the other's fear and determination, in spite of it, were too genuine to be doubted. I "Get out of sight—there, behind the window- curtains," the girl said.. "When I open the door this room must appear to be empty, in case anyone .should look in."

Sybil obeyed, hiding herself behind the long, musty-smelling drapery "of old-fashioned damask :that hung over one of the two windows. As she did so, the girl opened the door, peeping into the 'passage, then ventured further out, and noiselessly closed the door behind her. Moment after moment .passed, and she did not come back. I Sybil waited, with her blood singing in her ears; and, just as she was almost irresistibly tempted to open:Ahe door and look out at all hazards, her ,friend came flying back. Without a word—without even stopping for a glance at Sybil—she ran to the mantel where the lighted candle stood, and, standing on tiptoe, blew out the name. I "She is coming uptairs," the girl whispered, "and he is waiting below! We are lost—you And I! I might as well have left you where you were, and so have saved myself But if I had, I should never have known another peaceful moment; while now—anyhow, I've done thy best!" "Is there no way out of the danger?" breathed Sybil, shrinking close to the other in the dark, the acrid smell of candle-smoke strong in her nostrils. "If there is, I'm too frightened to think of it. She will find out that you are gone from that worn. If they had both come up, we might have ventured down, trusting to the night to slip away wifhout being discovered. But with him there, it would be no use. Or, stop; let me think. There might be a way; after all. There's just one chance in a hundred we might do it !" _ _

"What—wha ?" panted Sybil. "In another moment she will know that you have escaped. She'll run down to tell him, and then, in just those two or three minutes that. we shall have, we must make for the attic. They won't think of that; they'll guess that I must have helped you—though I hope they won't. discover the secret way—and they will believe we have gone, never dreaming that we are still hidden in the house. • Hark! Did you hear 'anything then, or was it only my fancy?" Sybil seemed to listen with her whole soul. The walls of this old house were thick, but she did hear something. At first there was an exclamation in a woman's voice, muffled by distance, 'then the slam- ming of a door, and, last of all, footsteps that ran along the passage. "Now-,-it must be now or never 1" th) girl exclaimed, desperately. She caught' Sybil's hand, hurried her to the door, and softly opened it. The passage was dark but from somewhere, far away, came a faint gleam of light. Sybil, yielding herself completely to the other's guidance, was drawn in the opposite direction. Only one who knew, the way almost by instiict could have gone so unerringly to a destination through the darkness. But Sybil felt herself conducted round corners, up two or three steps here, and down a few more there, until at length they stopped before a door. "The key of the attic is in the lock," her come panion said. "I hoped it might be, for there' nothing of value there. I'll take it out, and, if she sees it's gone, she will only think it has been lost. UP in the attic we are safe; l'm not afraid there. The trouble is that we can't stop long to starve; and how we're to get food, or how we're to get away, I don't know no more than you do." Almost noiselessly, though with a band that trembled, the girl withdrew the key; then, still guiding Sybil, pushed her towards the first step of a steep flight of stairs. Sv},il ban going slowly up, while behind her tho through which they had just come closed with a faint grating of the key in its lock, as it was inserted on the inside, turned, and taken out once more. The girl, who knew every cranny of the old house, ran up the winding stairs more quickly than Sybil ; and, though Sybil had started in advance, the other iyas almost instantly at. her side. "So far, so good!" she ejaculated. "I put the candle in my pocket, and I have matches, too. There's one big place under the eaves in the attic, where there's no window for ever so far, and we can dare to have a light. No one outside, looking up at the house, could see it. I remembered that when the idea came to. me that we might hide there."
Sybil could not answer. The mystery, the horror of the situation, gripped and held her as in a vice. The thought of a voluntary imprisonment.

attended by the pangs of starvation, such as sbe. already began to feel in a degree; the fretting misery of continuous suspense, to be. followed. perhaps, by failure, and discovery at last by that unknown pair of whom her friend spoke as "be" and "she," appeared more dreadful than remain below to meet her fate at once, whatever iu might be. But there was another to be considered—another who had apparently run great risks for her salEe. Besides, she herself had asked if there were other way of escape from danger," and, now the the way had been provided, it would indeed be ungrateful to complain. So, in silence, she allowed herself to be horrLe up a long flight of stairs that wound steeply to rer storey above. At the top her guide encircled 0r waist with an arm, and together—never lifting their feet from the floor, lest they should stumble 0 fall—they groped on and on through darkileeen,' sometimes coming into unexpected contact vrite li r. chest, or pieces of furniture piled one upon anoLu At last it was safe to strike a match and light tb,_ candle, which Sybil's guide had taken from ;I: stick in the room downstairs. It was already ba;'_ burnt, and, as Sybil glanced fearfully round at nderlitat; ue old boxes and old furniture stored away sloping roof, she dreaded the moment when, t„0 candle should be spent. But her friend intention of letting this calamity_happen for some' time to come. "When we have found a comfortable place tet.lipie' down, we'll put out the light," she said. "T,:e-oi are sure to be rats up here, and I am airs' rats, aren't you? But cnly one of us must sleeP at a time; so there will be no danger from theect even in the dark. Here, this hos is only straPeery not locked, and I know what's in it, for I been up here exploring hundreds of times, looked into every box and every chest of dtawier" • that I could open. There are two or three ust. cloaks in this queer old trunk that women ra,th. have worn generations ago. They're not wei;ei keeping, for the moths have got at them; but: will serve our purpose. We'll spread them on floor in that corner behind all the furniture, 01,7 the eaves, and call it a sort of bedroom. YOlic—hei we may as 'well make the best of things se are. "It seems very strange to be arrangle, conifortable bed," said Sybil, hc lung the 0011 while the other opened an ancient travelling-b04.5 leather, and proceeded to drag out its contes,o "Very strange, when you say we may never be abit to escape from this place alive. What does,_.4 matter whether we rest on cloaks or sit on the 0"-- , floor, if we are starving to death ? " "But we may not have to starve, and we escape, after all," retorted the girl with gipsY Lle6; "I've had a queer life, and I've learnt to philosopher. Already I've got some plans in ..70 head; and, now that we've the cloaks nicely sPA'",O on the floor, we'll put out the candle and tall ' over." The girl illustrated her words by the action had suggested. In a moment they were enveler;, in blackness again—the two, young creaturee to" strangely brought together clasping hands in echoing silence and darkness of the old attic. t "Will you tell me your name, and why you e firga brought me to this horrible house, then obelea your mind, and tried to help me get away ?" as . Sybil. . 'I told you that you mustn't ask ques,tie,ll% didn't I? But—well, it's different now. T°,,e`,.-01c nothing to do here for awhile but wait and nue over plans for escaping by-and-bye. There are things I don't mind letting you know; but, what do you suppose is happening downstairs? ,0 "They—whoever they ' may be—those t" people you talked about—are looking for neg maybe," Sybil answered, in an awed whisper. "Yes. One of them is looking, I am sure; not in the house. They will be certain that. had done one of two things—either that we irhe made for the boat which you and I left at river this afternoon, or else that we had gone the village. If I thought they were both searrhinle it would be easy enough for us to slip out house; but I am sure mother would not have elle' She is lame." +her "Your mother ? " echoed Sybil. "Is your , against you—and against me?" "She is only my stepmother really," exPlaill the other. "But I didn't know the truth abnea: myself so very long ago, and I have alwaYe Galles her my mother, though she has been Cruel an wicked to me, until lately, when she had reason tl think I could do something for her. MY name lb, Hester Frayne. If you and I live to call e9'e other anything, you nauat call me Hester, Piz' have tried to-night to be your friend. The MAYOR in proposing the adootion of the minutes, said the members of the Council would have read with some interest the very important report presented by Councillor A J Jo'ley—(hear, hear)---a report which showed the very decided interest he took in this impor- tant question, and which also gave a considerable amount of information as to how the Government pro- posals were likely to affect Warrington as originally submitted. They would have more to say on the matter later on. At present they merely received the report. Ceenciller GLIMNING seconded. The New Technical School.—Councillor Bennett's Final Protest.

Councillor BENNETT said that no allusion had been made to the feet of the work tog plans and perspective drawing of the new Technical School having been sub. mitted by the architects and approved. He thought they ought to he submitted to the Council before being adopted. He had a final protest against the site. He had always felt thst the site was a wrong one, prim- arily becauseithe site would probably ‘3(3 wanted eventu- ally for other purposes. He was still strongly of opinion that it would be wanted in the future. HA had seen the plans, and as plans he was not going to criticise them. Whether the plans were good, bad, or indifferent, or however excellent they might be. he still maintained that it would be utterly impossible for the building to look well on the particular site selected. They would spend anything from £15,000 to £30,000 on this erection but placed between two incongruous buildings, it would not be as effective as its cost and importance should make it. He might be accused of flogging a dead horse but he was strongly prompted to make this final protest. They would probably be sorry when the building was completed that they had selected the other site. Alderman gnaw GREEN said Councillor Bennett was making a mistake. This resolution applied to the com- mittee only. Tee committee approved of the plans. By and by the place would come up for the approval of the Council. There would then be an opportunity for objection, and, if thought necessary, their return. The Meson said that was so. The plans must be sub- mitted to the Council before the building was proceeded with.
Alderman SUTTON said that Councillor Bennett objected to this site. They were all aware that the site was unanimously chosen, and it was then in accordance with the desire of Councillor Bennett.

Councillor BENNETT :—t have objected on every posiible occacion. Alderman SUTTON ob+erved that be hal no doubt if there were twenty other sites Councillor Bennett would find something ,better than the one be now favoured. He (Alderman 'Sutton) did not think there was a b9tter site in %Varrington than the one selected. If it was not goad ecough for a technical institute he did not know what was. It was a valuable site in every region', and it was pe, fectly childish and absurd for anyone to be continually harping about it not being a good site and advocating a change to some other site. He objected to the whole of Councillor Bennett's_argument. _ _ _

CouncillAr MONIES said Councillor Bennett had been perfectly consistent in opposing the whole thing from the:commencement. Be had, howeyer,changed front in one particular. At first be said the site was not good onough,qnd now he intimated that it was too good. Be (Councillor Monks) on the general question still affirmed that the site was particularly suitable and lent itself in special ways to the work which was to be carried on in the Institute and Continuation Scheots generally. Under those circumstances he thought they had no option but to go on" with the plans prepared for the site. There was a minority of one in this matter. Mr. Owen ad- vised them to go on with this site, and he (Couacillor Monks) did not think they could do anything else. The MAYOR thought it was due to Coulcillor Bennett to say that he was not in a minority of one on this ques- tion. Regardine‘ the front elevation of the building, he (thee Mayor) had a good deal of sympathy with him.

Councillor' MONICA I meant practically a minority of one. (Laughter.) fhe :dawn said the point which had weighed with him in abandoning further oopasiti*n to the proposal of the eut-committee was the fact that the Committee had thoroughly thrashed the matter out, had taken into consideration the objections that Councillor Bennett and he had raised, and had come back after considerable deliberation and stated that under all the circumstances this was the best possible site they could choose for the purpose and was better for the plans than any other suggestions. Under those circumstances he felt iustifiei in sinking his own personal views, and agreed to the recommendation. He cordially approved of the Act,and he hoped the Committee would at once take steps to get rid of these things in an eqoitablb manner. Councillor F. R. ROBERTS did not understand why a minister s,lould receive 103 for a funeral in the morning and only 31. for one in cue afternoon. The tendency was to drive all the funerals to the afternoon, and they got a distinction between class and class which on these occasions was not desirable. They ought to equal .Z 9 the fees so that people belonging to the working, classes should be able if they wished to get the interment over in the morning. He saw no reason for paying a clergy- man 103. because the funeral happened to he in the morning. He should think many of them pre- ferred the morning, and in his opinion a maximum fee of Is. 63. would be ample for any clergyman either morning or afternoon. He did not know they could better afford to pay 103 in Warrington than could the people of Sale and Altrincham. where ' many rich men lived. div.head: BOERS AND
div.p: THE BOERS AND
British Military Authorities cut off the supply.

The Fortunes of War require that the Enemy should be harassed in every practicable vsray. His supplies of medicine as well as of food must be commandeered. Hence the amusing incident related in the following
CONFIDENTIAL LETTER from their Capetomm Agent to the Dr. Williams' Medicine Company :

"You will be interested to hear that during the Boer occupation of Aliwal North, the demand for Dr. Williams' Pink Pills was so great that in a very little time every storekeeper was 'sold out' of them, and the only Chemist in the place had to remove his enamelled sign, he was so much worried by our friends the enemy for "pink palitjes." Of course during that time the Military Authorities were careful that no fresh supplies reached Aliwal North or the surrounding country."
Dr. ,;\ illiamsi 'lnk Pills: WHAT THEY HAVE DONE FOR THE BOERS.
Dr. Williams Pink Pills:

The Dr. Williams' Medicine Company have received a great number of grateful letters from the Transvaal and Orange Free State since the pills were introduced into South Africa. Owing to the innumerable cures of our own countrymen and women constantly being effected, these have never been published before in this country, but the specimen following Is of special interest at the present time. Our energetic enemy has good reason to praise the strengthening and restorative powers of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills.
WHAT THEY HAVE DONE FOR BRITISH SOLDIERS.

The Dr. Williams' Medicine Company has, within the last few months, received numerous letters from British Soldiers, describing the universal use of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills in South Africa, where, before the war, 130cr and Briton alike relied upon them before all other remedies as the universal Household Medicine, and where they are one of the numerous commodities which the Doers have been deprived of by the ill-fortune of war. The latest letters are as follows :

Reserve Squadron, 12th Royal Lancers, Colchester, September 21st, rgoo. GFNTLEMEN,—I have great pleasure in forwarding you the facts of - a little incident which occurred to me personally during the recent operations in South Africa. On the x3th February last, while under Lord Roberts and General French, we surprised and captured the Boer laager at Klip Drift. I was one of the first to cross the Drift, and I noticed a portmanteau in the laager which the Boers had left behind in their flight. It was open, and on my examining the contents I found six small packages, wnich I opened and found to be bottles of your Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People. I distributtd them amongst my chums, and all informed me that they derived great benefit from them. I have just rejoined the Reserve Squadron of my regiment after a sick furlough, and there are many others here who can testify to the accuracy of my statement. _ _ .
You may make whatever use you like of this, as under the circumstances I think it right to acquaint you of the facts.—Yours faithfully, J. LARKIN (Trooper).

"The rheumatism at last attacked Me so badly that I was laid up in bed for three months in Potchefstroom, during which time I suffered agonies. I dared not move, the pains were so terrible. Fortunately I was in my fattier's house, and although my people did all they could I could not get relief. My appetite also left me, and altogether I felt that life was unbearable. Then a good Samaritan recommended me to try Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People. I had heard of many instances of their curative powers in the two Republics, and bought a box of the pills at a store. Very soon I felt the pains departing. In fifteen days I was able to get up, and felt much better in general health. My appetite returned, and I could enjoy my food. I continued Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for another three weeks, and by that time I felt perfectly well. I have never felt the slightest relapse or feared a return of that terrible, rheumatism. I once gave a friend of mine a box of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for his wife, who had been ill in bed for over a month; he wrote to me stfterwards to thank me, for she had been perfectly cured, and was up again and quite well."

(Hear, hear.) He (the speaker) would like to say a few words with reference to the Mayor's good wife. ( t.pplaese.) He thought she had endeared herself to everybody in Warrington. She had endeavoured during the past year to assist her hushand in every possible way, and Irrespective of position. re - ligion or anything else she had done what good she could in the interests of the town. (Hear, hear.) Therefore they might include in that resolution that their thanks be also given to the Mayoress. (Applause.) Couticillor Mons observed that he had much pleasure in secending the resolution. There was no :doubt that the feeling in Warrington was one of universal satisfac- tion at the uniform courtesy with which the Mayor had treated everyone, and the very full way in which he had carried out the duties of the office. Be was quite sure that the resolution was one which would heartily com- mend itself to every member of the Council. (Hear, heat.) Alderman FRaNCOM3 supported. He remarked that he was quite certain that the Mayor had given com pieta satisfaction. he had shown great ahility and had spent much time in doine, public work. He was pleased to hear that he would be re-elected unanimously on the 91h November, and he was quite sure that that was net only Ithe wish of those who held positions in the Council, but the wish of all outside the Coancil, and that he might have as successful a year next year. (Applause.) It was their hope that the Mayor and Mayeress would be both blessed with good health to carry on their work during the next twelve months. (Hear, hear.) Alderman SHAM GREEN also supported, and said he did not know that any mayor had had such a large amsunt of work to do. When he first entered upon the office there was a great amount of work to b 3 done, , which was, he was sure, a great e'rain upon him, but he never stinted himself with regard to time and energy, but fulfilled the duties efficientiy. They were proud to see him looking so well at the conclusion of toe mayoral year, and hoped that he and his wife would be fully equipped and prepare -1 to undertake the duties, which they expected to reimpose on November 9th. (Hear, hear.) COancillor GREENING said he w like to take that opportunity of personally thanking the Mayor tor the able and impartial manner he had discharged his duties. Not long ago the Mayor had a very trying time. They I knew what strong convictions the Mayor had on Ipolitical issues and it went without saying that no man I could have been more impartial outing a Parliamentary ielection than was the Mayor. (Hear, hear ) N,..t only I so, but he (Councillor Greening) personally took a pride in the fact that the Council bad been able to elect from their own body a gentleman who could es) ably fulfil the duties expected of him. (Hear. hear.) 0 a looking' over I the return of attendances he found that ti:e Mayor had put in no fewer than 255 attendances. 'that was something like 100 mere than anyone else. IC showed conclusively that the Mayor did not take offiee simply as a matter of form or honour, but to do, a+ he always had done sines he entered the °mined, real hard work for the benefit of his native town. He was glad the town was to have the Mayor's cervicei tor the next twelve months. Tae Mayoress had been referred to.aud he (Councillor Greening) had no dollar that much of the success of Alderman Rob.rts was &II to the advice which could only be given by a devered and loving wife. Cou cillor A J JoLLEY said possibly a word of criticism might add a little to the zest of tee proceedings. He would litre to suggest that during the Mayor's coming year of office he would not atteni public worship at churches and chapels in his official capacity quite so often as during the past year. It was not that he (Counaillor Jolley) thought the Council was past praying for—(laughter)—or even that the Counc I did not naed to be prayed for—but some of them had a strong obj .c- -don to tieing preached at. (Laughter). The DEPUTY-MAYOR then put the trintion to the meet- ing and it was unanimously agreed to. The MAYOR, in reply, said he was deeply indebted to the Council for the extremely handsome maneer in which they had put upon record their appreciation of his services during the past year. Whatever opini there might have been with regard to the Mayon ot Warrington everyone would agree that the town hie hien singularly fortunate with its Mayoress.:s. (Appiause.) As far back as he could rememoer the Mayoress of the Borough had been a lady who had endem, herself by her courtesy and amiability to every section of the community, and ha was persanally very much gratified that the Council had that evening ap preciated so kindly and in such exceedingly ple.s ant terms, the conduct of his wife during the pas., twelve months. AS Alderman Sutton and Councillor Greening had said, everything a woman could do to strengthen the hands of her husband its what had been a somewhat arduous year of office, she had loyally done. They all admitted that some hard wolk had been don., and, of course, the attendance he had made on committees proved that fact although it by ne means erTr.sented the total amount of public work. It was gratifying to find that the old adage that hard work did not kill was perfectly true. and if he was laoking, well he had to thank the members of the Corporation for the loyal support which had been given to him, which bad not ben exceeded in re- gard to any mayor who had preceded him. (Appl ruse.)

AMONG the Boer prisoners now safe in St. Helena is a man named Pot,gieter, formerly of the Railway Hotel, Potchefstroom, and a sturdy, active fellow he is, endowed with an intelligence and education far surpassing the ordinary stay-on-farm Boer. Some notes of a chat with Potgieter, taken two years ago by a press correspondent, are now reproduced, being important in revealing a glimpse of the hardships and pain that the Boer has to face equally with our own countrymen. "1 travelled a great deal in the Orange Free State three years ago," said Mr. Potgieter. "My business made it necessary for me to journey in carts and on horseback, often for months at a time, and, as I was out in all weathers, I frequently got soaking wet through, and had to let my wet clothes dry on me. I caught cold upon cold, followed at last by a severe attack of rheumatism. My legs and back only were affected at first, but by degrees the pains flew to the back of the neck and, in fact, all over my body. Doctors seemed powerless to cure me, so I gave up my Free State business and came to the Transvaal, first to Klerksdorp and afterwards to Potchefstroom, for further advice. In each town I consulted doctors, but without success. _

div.head: BLOEMFONTEIN.
div.p: BLOEMFONTEIN.
Bloemfontein, May 601,..zg00.

DEAR SIRS,—I thought that I would write and let you know what Dr. Williams' Pink Pills have done for me. I have been down with dysentery several days, and could get no rest. I read in the paper about your pills, and I thought that I would give them a trial. As I was not allowed out of hospital I got one of my chums to get me a bottle, which I gave 3s. for at Bloemfontein. I took them as directed; before I had finished the first bottle they gave me relief; the next bottle I was well enough to join my regiment at the front again in good health. There were one or two of my chums sick the same as I had been: they gave them relief. I have recommended them to all. I think they will help me to see the fight out; I shall never be without them again as long as I live. (3988) PRIVATE J. HORN, 7th Dragoon Guards, Field Force, South Africa.

div.head: MAFEKING
div.p: MAFEKING

Mafeking, Thursday, July 19th, 1900. SIR, —Having constantly used your valuable Dr. Williams' Pink Pills during the South African war, I always tound them to be of the greatest service to me, and I can highly recommend them to anyone who is exposed to the several diseases of this climate. Having just received one of your envelopes from my brother, who is at present serving at Lindley, Orange River Colony, I enclose the same to you, which will show the public that your valuable pills have been prized during this war. LCE.-CORP. MORGAN, Imperial Mounted Infantry. Munster Company. Ist Battalion R.M.Fusft

"The Golden Legend" is conceived on I grand scale. Here no parsimony is shown in levying upon the 1 resources of the modern orchestra, a noteworthy feature of the scare being the inclusion therein of a complement of four bells (4pecially cast for the purposes of this work and repreeentiug the bells of Strasburg Cathedral) and the liberal is,e which i.• made of such unusual instru- ments as a piccolo, bass clarionet, Eoglish horn, tuba, contrafa.geote, and two coreeta. And as we understand the Musical Society is bent upon a thorough and complete rendering of the Legend doubtless all these novel:ies will be found in next Wednesday's orchestra. From our advertising columns it will also be seen that the names of four vocalists of repute are announced for the prin- cipal parts. The prologne, as is suggested by the text, gives us an orchestral representation of the storm raging round the Cathedral during which Lucifer and the Powers of the Air are engaged in their sacriligioua on- slaught on the edifice. The bells here play an exceed- -1 ineiy important part and their effect is considerably en- hanced by the device of frequently causing the male VO'Cl3 to sins, their notes with chern,thus literally making thin " speak " To the female voices is, on the other hand, allotted the part of the contending evil spirits, the whole making up A most weird and realistic scene. The peculiarity of the music attending Lucifer's appearances is particularly striking. Whenever engatted in his asustned character of a physician, Sullivan has identified the part with some very formal and scholastic phras,s which cannot fail to attract attention. Early in the work and while Prince Henry is yet sojeutnin,,e in the humble abede of Ursula and Elsie occurs the most familiar choral excerpt of the work, the Evening Hymn "0, gladsome light" the moving quality of whose expressive unaccompanied harmonies conjoined to simple yet most effective me'nody ale destined for all time to profoundly impress the lis'ener. Elsie's pr. ser •I My Redeemer and Lerd " affords another illuktration of the composer's happy use of slinnlerneana, and here conspicuous use will be noted of the Cor Anylais. A fine opportunity falls to the part of Lucifer in the number in which he is engaged in flippantly imitating the chant of the pilgrims of whose wonderful pity and pall "he sings so derisively. Elsie's charming solo and the equally beautiful chorus to the same words "The night is calm and cloudless," usually brings to a close the first half of the pro- gramme. Some very dramatic situations are depicted is the music which follows. After another most 1 touchiog moreceau of unaccompanied choral harmony " 0, pure in heart "the music moves on to the exciting rescue of Elsie from the clutches of the Fiend, now masquerading in t• e guise of a Medical Friar, and here will be heard orchestra chorus and principals alike en- gaf.:el in the realisation of a most vivid and powerful , climax. The tranquil character of the music noticeable lie the subsequent delineation of the story comes out in strong relief by juxtaposition with what precedes it,and the final duet between Elsie and the Prince will be listened to with Cie rapt attention which its pesc,ful au i soothing beauties; cannot fail to command. The choral epilogue is well worthy oflattention, and it will he regrettable if this number should suffer, as it often does, from the confusion atten lent upon the premature departure from the hall of individuals in the audience. From a simple beginning a grand effect is built up, one of the leading instrumental melodies being here utilised for choral purposes in a spirited fugue which is finelF worked out. The fusion of all voices in a grand unison' passage marks so imposing eonOusion, alt reseurccs of cnorus orchestra and organ being hi re tully engaged in contribu:.ing to a fitting climax to a gl:rious woik. It 13 to be hopet that a hearty measure of public support will be accorded to this ainb tioua, yet in all respects praiseworthy and deserving, effort t) cater for our musical gratification.

div.head: PRICE:-OF MILK.
div.p: THE PRICE:-OF MILK.
Local Farmers Suggest an Increase

On Manday evening a 'meeting of the Lanisashire and Cheahire Dairy Farmers ot Warrington and the district was held at the N irton Army Ho! el. Warrington for the purpose of "establishing a dairy farmers' association and to promote the interea's of the dairy farmers of the dis- trict in general." There was a moierate atzendauce, over whie.h Mr. Einiu Btich presided. Tue UHAIRMAN explained that the prrsant gathering was the ou• coin- of a small ireAing held on Wedne:- day night last,. It was intended to torm an association ot some slit! Tne otj ct of the association was Co " improve ' the orica of milk, but before they could do that they wow,' nave " to lay the foundation stone, build up, and gr dually get to the top. The cost of labour was a very important Roan. In dairy farming it had advanced ten per cent. Cake and -tier feeding s'uffs had also advanced tan per cent., and that made twenty pr cent, on the xpenditure side of toe question. If the matter was fairly laid before the pobl c, he did not think they would wish farm- rs to pay 20 per cent. without some little addition beim! given to them in the shape of profit. (Hear, hear.) 0 le of the objec's they had in view was to improve the price of milk There were other objects which the association should promote, and he thought they might give the public to understand that it was not simp!y to improve the price of milk for which they had met. They intended to give the best qaalitv of milk, and they should have a fair price tor it. The public generally did not consider these important matters as much as they ought to do There was a great amount of nourishment in milk, it was abut the cheapest article of food on the market. It would compare very favourably with the price of bread. They might engage the services of a veterinary

surgeon who from time to time could visit the members of the association and,if they wished it,inspect farmers' stock. They did occasionally, in changing stock, come across beasts about which they were somewhat doubt- ful. Therefore the veterinary surgeon might give them a little valuable information at times• The Corporations of Warrington, Liverpool, Manchester and Stockport had very strong powers for dealing with cases ot this sort. Although a farmer might be a practical man a veterinary surgeon might be very valuabte to him. Then, he suggested, that an analyst should be obtained to ex- amine the cakes and food-stuffs, while a solicitor would give them valuable advice on most important points with regard to the law. Then the question of tuber- culosis and sanitary matters might be taken into con- sideration.

Mr WILLIAM BENNETT said he was present at some inconvenience to say a word or two for the benefit of his brother farmers. They were all agreed that farmers were producing one of the best articles (milk) which was consumed at a price below its value. Be did not see why that should be so, and he thought the public would not object to pay more. The milk dealers, he went on to say, had a meeting a week ago, and the majority of them were in favour of a rise, loot it was said the farmer had never asked for such a rise. The importance of providing pure milk was referred to, as well as several grievances, and he contended that tbey should form an associstion on the lines of that which existed in E,ses. The farmers there had an association and fixed the price of milk, and if a farmer happened to lose his milk customer he was indemnified against any loss during the time he was without that customer. That was a matter which required very earnest considera- tion. Now he was prepared to make an offer to the meeting, and that was that on a certain condition he would give £5O towards the start of the association. (Ap. nlsus,.) That condition was that if the meeting would find 103 farmers to subscribe a guinea each to form a special tund to fall back upon he would give £5O. (Ap• pia use.) .Then they coald form a strong association and indemnify any farmer who lost his customer. (A.polause ) _ _ _

Mr. J011;1 MAIZSII also addressed the meeting. and con- tended that farmers were not so well paid as they ought to be for their milk. They were satisfied on that question. Mr William Bennett, of Padgate, was unanimously elPcted vice-chairman, and the meeting appointed a committee, composed of Lancashire and Cheshire men, one from each township in the immediate district, to make arrangements for successfully carrying on the work of the association.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
The Golden Legend.

The Warrington Musical Society is shewing commend- able enterprise in venturing upon 4, first performance in the town of" The Golden Legend "for the opening con- cert of its season on Wednesday next. The work has long been recognised, by habituei of the concert-room in our larger estates of populatien, as one net only of great beauty and absorbing intflrest.but as. probably,the finest tning of its kind that its talented composer has yet given to us. Nor is the popularity of Sir irthur Sullivan's work surprising when it is recalled to bow charming a story his picturesque music is wedded. The levant as immor- t aiised in Longfellow's verse is, of course, the ground- work upon which the compsser has built up his musical picture, and the thrillinz interest of the story will be ad- mitted es a c mninon expsricnce. The exigencies cf a concert-room rendering have, in the nature of things, necessitated the elimination of all that is merely episodic in the teat alonz with a concomitant reduction of the leading characters to the conventional four. Noverthe- less Mr Joseph Bennett—who is responsible for prepar- ina the book—has admirably pres-3rved the pith of the legend, to refresh the the,mory of which the following summary of it will be useful.

The prologue discovers Lucifer engaged in conjunction with his attendant Evil Spirits in an impotent attempt to wreck the spire and other appurtenances of the Cathedral of Strasburg, the eefeat of the Prince of Darkness here fitly foreshadowing his final and corn- plii,te discomfiture. After this picturesqu3 intro Inc- tion Prince Henry of Hoheneck is, we are told, lying sick in body and mind in his castle at Vautsberg on the Kline and, having called to his aid the famous physi- cian of Salerno, learns that he can be cure i only by the blood of a maiden who shall, of her own fre3 will, consent to die for his sake. The Prince, regarding the remedy as impossible, gives way to dispair, when he is visited by Laeifer disguised as a travelling physician. The FJ-nd tempts him with . alcohol to the insidious influence of which he ultimately yields, with the deplorable result of lcsing his rank and of being driven forth as an outcast. Prince Henry is next found sheitering in the cottage of one cf his vassals whose daughter Elsie, moved by great compassion for his fate, resolves to make the rrquired sacral. e. The prayers of her mother Ursula being unavailing to turn her from hr purpose. Prince Henry, Elsie, and their attendants duly set out for Salerno. Oa taeir way th,y encounter a bani cf piigirms with whom is Lucifer dis- guised as a friar. He also is bound for the same desti- nation. On their arrival, the Prince and Elsie are received by Lucifer who has now assumed the form of Friar Angelo, a doctor oE the medical school. Elsie per- SiStEi in her resolve of self-martyrdom, despite the oppositi n of the Prince, who now declares that he intended only to test her constancy. Lucifer draws Elsie into an inner chamber, but the Prince and attend- ants, breaking down the door, rescue her at the last m-iment.
Miraculously cured of his malady Prince Henry marries the devoted E sie, and is restored to place and povicr.

In an appropriate epilogue a comparison is drawn be- twren Elsie's devotion and self-sacrifice, and the refreihing and fertilising influence of a mountain brcok in its cours from the c hills to the srid plain. THE talk is still of recon- A Reconstructed struction, but the process is Ministry. delayed and invisible, Some- body or something seems to be waited for, and we know not what it is. LORD SALISBURY keeps his own counsel. One day he is praised for his patriotism in consenting to still hold two offices in the Cabinet,aud another day he is plainly told that he must give up one or the other if he expects to keep his Administration in power and up to the level of national expectation. Ho has a number of old men in his Cabinet and he is instructed to get rid of some of them. AS he himself is an elderly man, this is a poor kind of compliment to pay him, and it ignores the fact that we have always had old men in our Ministries, and that they are the product of our peculiar system. The present Cabinet is one of coalition, and the fusion would be destroyed if a rigorous process of weed- ing out were commenced. New men and young are not available, and the cry for them is most unreasonable. A Government of young men would disappoint everybody. It would do too much, and in any Conservative Administration that is surely a bad quality. It would also amount to a Government by the permanent officials, of a more pronounced character than any we are likely to have under present arrangements. The demand for reconstruction, indeed, whenever it is urgently pressed, amounts to a vote of no confidence in the Ministry as it is, and Lord SALISBURY is not likely to be alert and prompt in responding to it. Why should he proceed to constitute a new Cabi- net? The inquiry has never been properly faced, and this accounts for the wobbling which is going on. The Cabinet has received the endorsement of the country. Its policy has been approved in the main. The contests were conducted about the was and its results, and the whole Cabinet was held to bo responsible. IG was not censured except in the Papers. Old Tories who supported it with grumbling did not take an effective way of giving expression to their views. They should have abstained from voting, or voted for Liberal candi- dates. Is it not too late to argue now that reconstruction is imperative P Who are the Ministers to be reconstructed out of the Cabinet. Lord LANSDOWNE is mentioned as one of them. But, apparently, he remains, and his successor has neither boon sought nor found. The " Times" says the present situation

will most likely be modified. "Lord SALISBURY is likely to seek relief from the burden of his dual office, and to hand over to a colleague the duties of the Foreign Secretaryship." Another journal, often well informed, mentions Lord LANSDOWNE as - the Foreign Secretary. A new Lord of the AA" miralty has to be chosen. It is open to sugges• tion, of course, that whatever changes are made•by putting old men into fresh offices will merely weaken the Govenment. The public has utterly lost confidence in one or two of the members of the Cabinet. It would like to see them retire,and quite new men take their places. Lord SALISBURY however, cannot be expected te make manY changes, and the suggestion that he should be a more energetic Premier comes as a reflection 00 his colleagues generally if they are old, and would be more necessary than ever if they were to be changed for younger men.

INTENSE interest is felt in America's Growth, the results of the North American census. It already announced that the total population of the United States has grown thirteen millions avid almost a quarter in ten years, and that is a signi' ficaut indication of enlargement beyond the rate at which population can possibly increase in the Old World. The citizens and their families, the negroes and the red men now total 76,295,220 souls. The conditions are not all known, end cannot be dealt with until we have the more cora- plete returns. We shall want to know how maul foreiga-born habitants have been added in the ten years, and whether the black population " growing faster than the white. It will be inter- esting to see whetherlthe large old towns araaU menting at a rate uut of all proportion to the newer large towns, and whether the Eastern, th 3 Western, or the Southern States are increal ling at the old relative rates, or some novel way. The statistics of the great cities have been already published, and enre3 of the Western prophets have been greatly dia" appointed by their results. It will be important also to know what are the proportions of the native and the foreign-born Americans, and hoW the Irish and the Germans are progressing in their relations to the other foreign immigrants. Tha American people are undergoing some great changes. The early American type, beloved 0' the caricaturist, is rapidly passing away. Adraiv ture of race, some changes of diet and habits, the leisure that money gives, and the increafie of athletic amusements, are creating quite a new type, an the spare, tail, cadav: Jug Wei/ and women, with sallow comp'exions 110 nasal voices, aro rapidly disappearing. Whell there were recruits wanted for Cuba the men who offered themselves were of the verl finest physique. They endured great hard" ships, and they came well out of the ordeal, if they suffered almost as much from sickness afterwards as the recruits of the Old World do under similar circumstances. The abundant food in America and the ge od wages stimulate the growth of the people in better physique, and the settlement of the Western lands seems to offer to all classes of the people admirable chances for re covering bodily health and vigour. A etwrg American nation is the result, and its strength has impelled it a little in the direction of an out-: side policy which has been called Imperialism, and will next week be submitted to the judgment ef the electors. The domestic development of Ode people of the United States has never cease, to be remarkable. Their local gO vernmen has been improving, and their means of educao" tion, always good, have been steadily hee°lllini" better. In their universities and their literature they have signally advanced. They believe if: education as a means to an end, and they; ere lie, bothered with a State Church and the rivalries the creeds. Unhampered by traditions and Cl prejudices, they produce excellent men and wonaeo, and their books and magazines hold a high Place in the world's literature. Emphatically a stron and virile nation, the great question is g whether they are to have sympathies of race, law. guage, and religion forcible enough to bring theo into line with Great Britain, and to give theta a wise, cool, elevated foreign policy. A great future is ahead of them, and they can only mar it by CO ruption, political stupidity, and a mad desire,: make money at all costs. Otherwise, their grovit will continue to beone of the marvels of the ti'e'

div.p: throne itself was found, and on different walls, or in detached pieces on the floors, were frescoes which are said to givo the first lively representation yet folind of the race which developed so early a civilisation impregnated with the spirit of art and the joy of life. Nor do the discoveries extend simply to the Greek period, !osculating as that is to moderns; but the immense antiquity of the settlement was re- vealed by an under-deposit containing unmistak- able traces of the Stone Ago. Intense must have been the delight of the explorers also when, after Clearing the entrance of the Dictt-ean cavern, according to Hesiod and Virgil the very cradle of Jupiter, a profound abyss was discovered, set with stalactitic pillars, crowded with votive offerings— the holy of holies.
