Recently there has been an agitation in several of the districts around 'Warrington for cheaper r,ailway facilities with this town on Market days. It is customary on many of the railway systems— no doubt the companies have found it advan- tageous to themselves—to issue cheap tickets to taarket towns on specified days. This has proved a great boon to many country people who are thus afforded a cheap means of reaching a market for the sale of their produce. Already some of the neighbouring villages are in the enjoyment of this Golborne people, for instance, are now ftole to reach Warrington on market days at a Con- 81derably cheaper rate than the ordinary are and other outlying townships are similarly favoured. It is, perhaps, only natural that those Who have been left out in the cold should appeal to the railway companies for more favourable treatment. Last week the Preston Brook, Dutton, -Aston and Sutton Parish Councils are forwarding a joint petition to the London and North Western Railway Company for cheap market tickets be- tween Preston Brook and Warrington on Wednes- days and Saturdays. Some of the authorities of local parishes served by the Cheshire Lines Rail- way might also find it to their advantage to make a like application. Warrington is now the most important market tawn in South 'West Lancashire and by affording cheaper means of reaching it, the two railway companies are likely to be the gainers in the long run.

London folks and provincials have in the return of the City Imperial Volunteers a common ground for jubilation, and the welcome in the country When the time comes will be'quite as hearty and sincere as it has this week been in the Metropolis The citizen soldiers who voluntarily left civil em- ployment and went out to South Africa, at a criti.. cal period in the history of war, placed the whole of the country under a lasting obligation, and the great influx of people to London on Saturday and Monday. evinced that the public generally are far from being unmindful of the valuable service which has been rendered by the Volunteers. The public, have been reminded, in more than one quarter' that the contingent which landed on Saturday at Southampton are few in comparison with the forces, composed of men of all arms, regulars as weil as Volunteers, who have a claim upon the gratitude of the English people. True; but, so far as the public are concerned, it is recognised that the volunteers are especially entitled to the feeling of gratitude. The Volunteers were not obliged to leave their homes to incur the risks and hardships of war, and. the chief, if not the sole, motive which impelled them was a patriotic desire to uphold the honour of the British flag. Nor is it too much to say that their spirited action has had an influence throughout Europe; and it may be added, more- over, that the endurance and soldier-like qualities of the Volunteers came as a revelation to represen- tatives of other countries in South Africa, and to some of our own military critics at home.

There is one fact in regard to the recent elec- on, as pointed out in the " Times " by Mr. Allan Bright, late Liberal candidate for Exeter, that really ought not to be lost sight of. The fact is, that for the first time within a century the peace Party have maintained their ground at a general election held during or shortly after a serious war. In 1812 the " peace " Whigs who had protested against the Peninsular War were for the most part Unseated. Romilly, Brougham, Tierney, Homer, William Lamb, the principal leaders of the Opposi- tion to the war, lost their seats. The Government Of Lord Liverpool gained between thirty and forty seats. In 1857, after the Crimean War and on the 19Pea1 of Lord Palmerston on the China question, the small" peace "party in the House of Commons Were annihilated by the country. Cobden, Bright, Alilner-Gibson, W. J. Fox, and Miall all lost their Beats, and Palmerston was returned with an in- Freased majority. In the late election, as far as can De seen, the peace party, as such,have kept up their numerical strength, while some of the members w„ere actually returned with increased majorities, 'ir Wilfrid Lawson, Mr. Stanhope, Mr. Maddison VA some others lost their seats, while, on the other riand, Mr. lieir Hardie, Mr. Richard Bell, and Mr. nrrie Grant, with less 'prominent "peace " men, won seats from the supporters of the war. But the Personnel remains somewhat altered.
In certain p:osecutions of dairy-men before

Devonshire magistrates for selling Devonshire cream containing boracic acid, used as a preservative, Dr. Stevenson, the specialist, gave evidence to the effect that such acid in cream, unless usedin minute quantities, has a very injurious effect on the health both of children and adults, producing skin erup- tions, vomiting, and even heart failure. Dr Diplock, of Chiswick, said that since February he had attended more than a hundred children, all of whose ailments he attributed to the fact that the milk or cream with which they had been fed con- tained boracic acid. Only in one of the cases now before the Bench was a conviction obtained, and in that no fine was imposed.

Farmers who have been deploring the exhaus- tion of nitrate deposits and the dearth of nutri-1 meat for the soil may take heart of grace. There is hope for our neighbours in country places, as vrel as for market gardeners, and allotment holders. Science is to speedily supply Nature with the re- quisite fertilisers, and crops are to grow apace, I almost defying the rigid limitations and necessities of changing seasons. For Nikola Gesla, whose high authority has hithertof ore been freely acknow- ledged, assures us that soon will electricity supple- ment and increase human energy by supplying us with pure water and nutritious food in abundance. By means of the scientific apparatus which he has invented he will extract and secure nitrogen now floating unchecked in the atmosphere, and will compel it at his will to fertilise the most barren soil The wilderness and the solitary places are to begin blossoming into fruitfulness by a modus operana'i which is simplicity itself. By means of a small brush discharge. he will set fire to the nitro- gen of the atmosphere:and will oxidise it to an un- limited extent. The results of such process will amazingly increase:the productive power of the soil and will cause nitrates to be unnecessary.

"The way of the transgressor is hard ;" and Judge Gwynne James evidently intends that the way of the debtor shall be so too, for at the Court House, Runcorn, on Tuesday, he intimated :—"rhis previous order in judgment summonses had been for seven days. He found, however, that where the defendant was arrested on a Monday, and lodged in prison, he was let out on the following Saturday. Thus instead of the seven days, the prisoner only got five days. In future his com- mittals would be for eight days." This new order should have a salutory effect and ba an inducement to the debtor to pay up.

I learn that Mr. E. Liaison, C.C.. and Mr. James Pritchard two of our highly respected townsmen have been elevated to the lagietertal Bench. That the townspeople will be pleased is very evident for both gentlemen are ardently admired in the circles within which they move as business men, as both upright and capable. Naturally, before either can be of real service in their new capacity, they will be required to extend their knowledge of magis- terial law, but this we do know, botu Mr Imisoa and 'Mr Pritchard have a large fund of commonsense and business acumen and have shown on more than one occasion they can apply it. Magisterial Benches, as is well-known, are never too richly stocked with such men, and we feel thankful to the Lord Lieutenant for adding two such useful gentle- men to the list of our magistrates.
The model of the propoged Transporter Bridge in Runcorn is now on view at the Town Hall, and is w#All worth inspection. In general appearance it is tat of a su3pension bridge pure and sinple.

The Rev Cation Wood, on Sun -lay evening list in the course of a sermon upon" The time ot Visita- tion,' made a slight allusion to the possibilities of a time coming when the Church of England as by law established would ba severed from the church It would not be exactly fair to affirm what the Rev Canon implied, but it would be interesting to know whether he holds the opinion that if there is to be a severance at all, it should CDOI9 when the friends of the' Church—The Tory Government—were in power?

div.head: SIR JOHN BRUNNER AND TH CHURCH OF ENGLAND. The Appointment of Pastors. Growti7-07-Ereeds.
div.p: SIR JOHN BRUNNER AND TH CHURCH OF ENGLAND. The Appointment of Pastors. Growti7-07-Ereeds.

On Sunday night, Sir John Brunner, M.P., president of the British and Foreign Unitarian Association, pre- sided over a meeting at Matthew Henry's Chapel, Chester, in celebration of its bicentenary, and promised t) bear the expense of erecting in the chapel two staine glass windows with portraitu in the centre of Mathew Hoary and James Martineau.

In the course of his opening pencil Sir John alluded to the differences in the Church of England, and said he bad been asked to support a Bill which had already be brought into the House of Lords by the Bishop of Rochester. One part of that Bill appeared to seek to endow the laity with a real voice in the appointment of their pastors—(hear,hear)--but it was tube within the limits-of the Church order. If that Bill came into the House of Canamons,and he found its power so restrict xi, be should feel very strongly inclined to move an amend- ment that the power be not confined within the Church order. If the laity were endowed with abso- lute and not limited power to appoint their own pastors, it would be a great step towards freedom in religious matters. He had dreamt of a new reforma- tion, and erhaps the best way was that they should try to remind their friends of the Church of England what it was they believed, or rather what it was they officially believed, or believed they believed. He found vary few knew what they did believe. Their offilial beliefs had grown from century to century through the operation of what were called Church C)uncils. He b,- lieved that, just as Martin Luther was cured of his belief in the Catholic Church by going to Rome, so it might cure a good many in the Church of England of the wish to believe what they were bound to believe if they only knew why it was they believed it, because those councils were verylmuch like political caucuses to-day, where there was continual int-zit:an from one side to another to obtain a majority, and all things down in the Creed to- day were all the result of chance majorities.

div.p: THE EX AAIN ER, FRI DAY, NOVEMBER 2, 19001
THE COWS MID TO WAIT.

What might have been a serious tr:cid,-,nt, but which happily only terminated in a comedy, was that which happened to a maa named Orred, employed on the Prospect Farm, Halton, the other day. It appears that he went up to the loft to obtain food for th 3 cows in the stalls below when suddenly the flooring gave way, and Ira was precipitated half way into the room below. One leg in particular was imprisoned in the bola made, and though he called for assistance, and struggled to gat free, it was not until about 1 hours afterwards he succeeded by his own efforts. In the.meantime the caws had been quietly chewing the cud, and silent spectators to the whole, were amusedly conte.t to wait for their feed.

THE MISSING RUNCORN- WOMAN, —BODY FOUND. Mrs. Lucy Littler, wife of Mr. William John Littler, Bentinck-street,Runcorn, who was reported missing from her home on Saturday, Octobsr 20!.h, has been traced. Tao circumstances are, how,ver, very lamentable. On Tuesday afternoon last, Cm- stable Ridgeway, of Satton Weaver, found the body of a vvomm floating in the Bridgewater Canal at Preston Brook. Information was conveyed to Run- corn, and general fears were entertained that it was the body of Mrs. Littler,—&t the inquest, held by Mr Coroner R Dobson, on Wednesday, Mr Littler appeared and identified the body as that of his wife. She was 31 years of age. Lately she had been in low spirits consequent upon troubles which affected her respecting the weaning of bar infant baby aged three months. She had four children the eldest of which was seven and the youngest the baby referred to.—There was no evidence to prove how the deceased got into the canal, and the ; jury returned an open verdict of "Found drowned." Much sympathy is expressed with Mr Littler and his family.

FOUNDERING OF A ILU'NCORN FLA.T•

On Friday night a fiat, belonging to Mr It Abel, foundered during a storm off Speke beach. It appears that the waves dashing over her caused her to drag the anchor and soaaihed in the hatches. She was driven with great force on Speke beach, where she fillel and sank. The men were compelled to take to the rigging, and were without fool for over 20 hours. They were lashed to the rigging for seven hours, and were rescued on Saturday after- noon by a passing steamer. Nlr J Stubbs, foreman of Mr R Abel's yard, with a gang of men visited the scene of the disaster on Saturday midnight, and got out of the hold, part of the cargo, bringing the flat eventually to Runcorn. The damage as estimated to be between £2OO and £3OO. FATALITY AT A WIDNES WORKS.

Last Friday, at the Accident Hospital, Nit Jones. deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body of Thomas Lunt, aged 19, who resided with his parents at 3, Lathom-street, and who was killed on Thurs. day at the soap works of Messrs William Gossage and Sous.—Patrick O'Neil said the deceased was in the employ of the London and North-Western Rail- way Company, and his duties were to remove boxes of soap from the loadinp-stage into the waggons, On the morning in question deceased had assisted to load some of the waggons, and witness gave the signal to the driver of the train to draw out. When the train had started, the deceased, who had to go to another portion of the works, lumped on to the end portion of one of the waggons. lie fell back- wards, and witness caught hold of his shirt, bu; he could not stick to him, and he fell b wean th,, waggon find the stage. He was twisted round and fell under he next, wfiggons,.the wheels of which went over hicn.—Nfr Farina, who appeared on behalf of to London and North-Western Railway Com- pany, produced a circular, of which deceased had had a copy, warning employ 63 of the company not to get on or off moving trains.—A verdict of" Acci- dental death" was returned.

div.p: SONS OF TEMPERANCE, RUNCORN.

The usual meeting of the above order was held in the Greenway-road schools on Saturday evening. The President, Mr Thomas R Whyte, occupied the chair. At the opening of the meeting the chairman and several officers expressed their satisfaction at the improvement in the health of Mr T Cooke, one of the officers of the division. The discussion on Lord Peel's minority report on the licensing ques- tion, which was a ljourned from a previous meeting, was resumed. Mr Thomas 3- Holt opened with an interesting speech, in which he warmly supported the recommendations of the report in the interests ed. temperance. He reviewed the history of the movement for the past 25 years, and said that while there was something to discourage, on the other hand there was much to stimulate them in the work, especially in reward to the enlightened public opinion on the question. Mr. Samuel Tomlinson also supported legislation on the lines of the report. Mr Alfred Hoden emphasized the importance of educating the young in the day schools onthe scientific aspect of the question. Much, he said, depended on teaching the young life of the nation. The discussion was then adjourned to the next meeting. RUNCORN 11A.B.RIEES DEFEATED.

The Runcorn Harriers entertained Warrington Harriers at Runcorn on Saturday. Added interest in the run was brought about owing to the large number of supporters who had journeyed to Run- corn with the football club. Runcorn, on the evi- dence of the last three weeks, were confident of victory. The visitors decided on a mile break,which came as a surprise to the borne team. The route tmken was in the direction of Hallwood, returning by Halton Brook home again, after a run a about five miles. A mile break was formed at Helton Brook. The first to breqk away was S Hopkins, closely followedhy M McDonald,of the visitorg.and W Lewis, of the home team. From start to finish the race was keenly contested, McDonald just beat- ing Hopkins for first honours. The remainder of the teams rolled in as follows :—Warrington: 1, McDonald ; 4. Dagnall ; 6, Ford ; 7, Price; 8, Ander- son—total, 26 points. Runcorn: 2, Hopkins; 3, Lewis ; 5, Goodall; 9, Stubbs; 10, Matthews—total, 29 points. Warrington thus won by three points. He could give no judg- ment upon it.—Subsequently when sitting in the large court, Mr Efindley appeared and told his Honour that he had sent a telegram to the Registrar of the Court saving that he would not be able to appear before 12 o'clock. The "wire" it was asce-- tamped instead of being sent to the Court was left at the office in High-street, although a notice was posted upon the door intimating that the office would be closed during the sitting of the Court. The judge under these circumstances allowed Mr Hindley on giving notice to Messrs Linaker and Linaker, to have the case reinstated at the next court.

div.head: 'TRH RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: 'TRH RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB.

The members of this club were on Tuesday even- ing treaed to an admirable and powerful address by Mr Whitehead, of Manchester. on "Land Taxa- tion." The chair was taken by Mr Joseph Brown, of Runcorn, who, whilst apologising for the absence of Mr Collie (Liverpool;, said he had seat a good substitute in his place. The lecturer dealt with the history of land taxes commencing with the feudal days, and the time when the land was given to earls and barons for services rendered, and when the old " hundred principles " were set up. Re spoke also of the restoration of Charles the II , during which time the landlords tried to get off finding a hundred yeomen. They wanted to pay a tax instead ; hence the land tax was created. This was practically continued until 1660. In the time of Villiam and Mary (1692) commenced what might be called the transfer of taxatiol from land on to necessities. When the land tax was instituted,the amount was 43 in the 2, but now it did not exceed id; thus,it would be seen, that the landowners have now almost entirely escaped the taxation, it W 45 intended they should pay. Ile coneiderei it an injustice that necessities should be S 3 heavily taxed, whilst the land, which was the natural pro- perty of the State. and ought, therefore, to be a valuable asset of the State, contributed little or nothing to the revenue. lie would rather go back to the original idea and let the land bear the taxa- tion of the country.—Throughout the lecture was listened to with marked attention, and at its con- clusion votes of thanks were accorded both to lecturer and chairman, —Next Tuesday' Mr Joseph Brown will lecture on Education, the chair being taken at 8 o'clock. Mr niveton also sang the solo" Mavy," with impressive effect.—Mr J Burkett contributed two readings, °lle on "Cheese," by Jerome B Jerome—which convulsed his audience with laugh- ter, the other—" I wish I hadn't." Both pieces were rendered in Mr Barkitt's usual splendid style. A. very delightful feature of the programme was the appearance of eight little girls from St John's—in two musical drills—conducted by , Miss Warburton and Miss Pritchord. The. first 1" The fan drill," was executed with graceful simplicity and sweetness—the second piece—" The little housemaid," raised most enthusiastic applause whieh could oulv be satiefled by an encore. Great 'Credit is due to Miss Warburton and Miss Pritchard for their admirable training of the children, One of the little girls—Miss Barnes—sang a very amuse- jug child's song, entitled "The Mouse Trap." Her sweet face and pretty accent drew a warm expres- sion of appreciation from the audience. Mr Frank Littler recited two pieces, "Ile who saved St Michael's." and "Pit Bits" in his usual impressive I manner. Mr Hill contributed two solos, "Anchored" and " Linger Longer," the latter was par- ticularly well rendered. Mr Hill's native sense of humour shone out conspicuously. Miss Amy Hill sang in a sweet and steady voice the solo " Astore." The Rev W A Eyre gave a very interesting address on "Congrega- tional Memories." The interval for refreshments was keenly enjoyed ; every eatable being bought up. A delightful evening terminated with a Wee thanks and the Doxology:

div.head: From Brindley to the Transporter Bridge.
div.p: From Brindley to the Transporter Bridge.
Lecture by Mr. W. Handley.

The new wing at the Runcorn Technical Institute, was filled to overflowing on Tuesday evening last, when Mr. William Handley, J.P., chairman of the Runcorn Urban District Couccil, delivered a lecture on" The his- tory of the Runcora Ferry." Toe chair was taken by Mr. S. Pope (chairman of The Free Library Committee), and he was supported on the platform by the Lecturer, Messrs. D. Bisbrown, and F. W. Hutton. Mr. W Handley, who was warmly received said he would endeavour tc.. give them "The history of an ancient Ferry." (Hear. hear.) The ancient Ferry be- tween Runcorn and Widnes will ere long be retnem- to:red amongst the things " which were, and are not," and a recital of its history, stretching back for more than seven centuries, may well claim a more than pass- ing notice. Prior to the establishment of the Ferry as a regular and erganizsd means of communication be- tween the counties of Lancashire and Cheshire, the bed ot the river Mersey at Runcorn gap was an important highway. The broad estuary of the Mersey Shea of much greater expanse, here suddenly narrowed ; beieg contracted by the out-cropping of the sandstone rock on either side, to a width of about four hundred yards, at high water, and less than three hundred yards at low water. Intercourse between the two sides of the river was then only possible by fording at low water over its sandy bed, and walking or riding through its shallow pools, which the swiftly ebbing tide had failed to carry away to the lower reaches of the river. During the cen- turies of the Saxon period this comparative isolation would be an undoubted advantage, as here the kingdoms of Mercia and Northum- bria confronted each other in grim array, and readier means of crossing would be considered undesir. able if not dangerous to the common weal, and an encouragement to engage in those laternecive quarrels between the kings of the Saxon Eleptarchy, whicte were so frequent as to be loeken upon-as a necessity. Con- figuration of the river at this sp3t also constituted it a kind of natural and easily protected gateway, which properly fortified barred the entrance of the pirat'cal Danes to the rich country which lay tehind. These con- joint • circumstances gave a character to the situation from which the Saxon fortress on Castle Rock, Runcorn, and the later Norman Castle on Halton Hill derived their origin and importance. The Normen conquest brought about many and far reaching changes—witu the avowed object of achieving its sabjugation, breaking up the remnant of the Sexon sympathy and power, and establishing the Norman suprem- acy and rule,—the whole county was divided into feudal districts and placed miler the control of powerful Barons, responsible not only for rendering military service to Earl and King, but also, for the government and loyalty to the new order of their vassals in their respective Baronies. Halton on the Cheshire side and Widnes on the Lancashire were each created a Barony, but within a period of about fifty years, these two Baronies were united, in the person of William Fitz Nigel, the second Baron of Halton, he hay- lug. married the eldest daughter wee co-heiress of the Baron of Widnee. At his death, having no son to succeed him in the title and estates, the Barony was divided between hie two daughters. This union of the two Baronies would undoubtedly make for peace and Beetrrity, and create the need for more frequent intercourse which the ferd acro:s the bed of the Mersey with its intermittent opportunities and dan- gerous possibilities did not provide. or a further period of another fifty years John Fitz Ricbard,the sixth Baroe, holding also the position of Constable of Cheshire provided a boat in which any so desiring might c , across the river. The establishment of the ferry at Runcorn is recorded in two deeds or charters which I believe are still in existeace the second being dated the year 1190. Both charters state the ferry as having pre- viously been established. John Fitz Richard succeeded ' his father in the year 1172. He appears t) have been a man of broad and enlightened views, a man of culture, and a patron of tVence as it is stated by Sir Peter Leycester that " John the constable of Cheshire had a clerk named William an excellent astrologer who in the year 1183 writ of the conjugation of the planets that year." John was also a brave soldier and ot such proved capacity and trust that Henry the Seccied seat him to Ireland in 1131 as Governor or Lord Lieutenant during the recall of Hugh Lacy, who had incurred the King's displeasure. Some time after his return John volunteered his services to Richard Cceur Da Lion and proceeded to the Holy Land as one of his Barons in the third crusade. Whilst so engaged he lost his life during the Beige of Tyre in toe year 1190: But to return from this, though necessary digression. The first deed or charter recites a grant from Richard de la More to his son and his heirs of "two boates of land in Reacover, late the lands of Beatrix of Higher Roacover " and also of " two parcels of land in Weinesse " which John the Constable of Chester had given him, with other lands, elasted with the obligation to pay to the " Hospital of S. John of Jerusalem at Lady Day the sum of two shillings yearly, and to find in the love of God one half of the necessaries for the passage of the ship of Widneees for, aver for all those wha should. pass. over. the river." RI would seen that the other half of the maintenance of the" Snip of eViduesee " was left to be provided by voluntary benevolence or from those" who should pass over the ,river." The second charter whicu bears the date 11D0 recites a grant from Gamier de Naplouee, the grand prior of the English Brotherhood of the Knights Elo;pitallere of the Order of Sc, John of" certain parcels of `land to Rie,harride le More and his heirs in consideration af his peyine 'four shillings yearly at Michaelmas and keeping in repair on the River Mersey at Runcorn the vessel which John che constabtefor the love of God had formally preceded to carry across the river those who desired it, upon con- •dtition that one third of tiee 'chattels of Richard and his heirs in succession at the death of each were reesrved to the brotherhood for the good.ef his soul." This latter • condition quaintly suggest thet the Prior knew how to snake a -profitable bargain and reveals the shrewd man -of business quite as exach as the astute ectaesiastic. Who was Richard de Moo? Why did latteand not Sohn ecake the grant for the maintenance of the Ferry ? Who was Beatrix and why was she mentioned? Why are the knights Hospltallers of the order of St. John. et Jerusalem included as beneficiaries en the two chestess ? And why should a foreign moabiele military Prior take such an interestein the Ferry at Runcorn as to ratlike a special grant of land in its favour? These questions, naturalise suegest themselves andttheir C 331-, perative examinatien and rprobable solution throw a floodszof light on the early history of the aneent Ferry. The Barons of /Salton held their Baronial tenure by military service ant as we have seen were, in such tur- bulent times, often awaymith their escUiree and re- tainers from their Barony accompanying the Earl nr King in their mnitary-expeditious or engaged in the wok of consollating the Norman rule and power. John, was also in three yeare after his accession sent on inepertant political service to Ireland, and a deputy wocid require to be left in charge as seneschal or steward of else Barony. in an earlier &atter connected with lXalton occurs the name of Richard de Is More as one of its witnesses. Be would probably be a relative ifxret a son of the then Baron and 'from this fact probably the steward; butwa have it re- corded that the second -son of John was surnamed De la More, and the township of More given him as bis por- tion, Being the younger son Sir Richard would be very naturally likely to occupy the position of seneschal or , steward- This hithel more probable as eCichard was SolEcted.with a leprous disease and therefore unfitted for ,military service. tit is eldest brother Rodger who succeeded John as the seventh Baron, like his predecessors tlevoted his energies to mili- tary service and so distinguished himself as to be accounted the first of the Barons; exciting both the fear and favour GC the King, who sent him on important nailitary service in Normandy, in the execution of which he gained the especial commendation of tbeirrench King for his prowess and indomitable courage. Richard ue la More would therefore 'in the absence of his father per- form the duties ant obligations of the Barony, and legal documents would probebly be made out in his name or by him as its executive officer. Selo fourth Baron, grandfather of tiebn married as his second wife Beatrix de 'Vessel, a 'lady of wealth, and pore- seseed of large estates in her own right. From the mention or itesoeladon of the natneffieatrix in theefirst charter it seems 'reasonable to icier that the wife of the 4th Baron is here iindicated, and-that John's as successor in the Baronyiinherited her lands in Higher Roncever, and that he vested them in the person of Richard de la More as trustee, charged with the partial support of the Ferry, and the payment of the stipulated sum to the hospital of St John t orusalem onresedy Day in each year. (It may be bube coincidence but it is notewerthy thac the charch situate el Raneorn Hill, the enceeeeer or a mech aernerchurch is dedieisted to St Meryl. Richard wishful to fulfil his trust he letter as well as spirit, knowing that his fell disease might at any time incapacitate him for the due performance of any legal ace, roused on his true: to his son, and his heirs charred with the obligation of its special provisions. In this Richard showed wisdom and forethought, for though he lingered on in weakness and suffering he died a few years afterwardsoind was hurled in the chapter house at Norton Priory. It is pleasing to know chat in an aee, often described by the historian, " as drunk with the lust of war and cruel oppression " that the silent appeal of the suffering of the leprous Richard de Is More so moved the heart of his brother Rodger that he endowed a house On the hanks of the Ribble, which he had inherited

from his maternal ancestors as a leper hos- pital, wfth a quantity of land for its maintenance. This is the more noticeable as Rodger is described SS of so fierce a character as to have earned and twen known by tha unenviable surname of Rodger "Hell." The second charter or deed which was made by Gamier de Naplouse provi,lei for tbs reptir of the ferry boat and also added an additional grant of money, payable at Michmlinas in inch year to the Hospital of St. John. Coupled with the somewhat singu'ar condition as to the re7ersion of

one third of the goods and chattels of each successive De la More at his death. The Knights Hospitallers and the Knight's Templars were two semi-religious, semi- military organizations which were born of the pilgrim- ages to the Holy Land and the wars of the Crusaders. The Hospitallers adopted St. John of Jerusalem as their Pateon Saint, and attached thetnselves to the Monastic Order of St. Augustine, wearing their dress—a white tunic and a black mantle en which they added as a dis- tinctive symbol a white cross with eight points. As their name and the name of their Patron Saint implies they were given to acts of hospitality and works of mercy rather than to the art of war. The Knights Tempters were the more militant order. They attached themselves to the Benedictine order of Monasticism. They wore over their tunics a , white mantle adorned with a large red cross on I the left breast, shield, and banner. From these distinctive marks of dress they were named, the white cross and the rod cross knights'. 'rho Augustide Priory established at Runcorn by the second Baron of Halton in 1133 was with its church probably contiguous tu the Ferry. Its situation on the 'sank of an ofticaes turbu- lent river, with its uncertain fords, suggested St Christopher as an appropriate patron saint, and on the removal of the Priory to Norton, a few years subse- quently, a huge figure of St Christopher was set up un- der a canopy in front of the Monaltry, he being believed to have stormy rivers and those de- siring to cross them under his special care. John the sixth Baron had a younger brother named Robert. He adopted the Monastic Order of St. Augustine, indeed most likely being one of the fraternity located at Norton. He had for many years been the grandmaster of the Knights Hospitallers in England, being appointed to that office in the year 1150 some 15 years earlier than the appointment of Gamier de Naplouse as grand Prior in 1165. It will therefore be readily conceded from this chain of circumstances. that though John is recorded as the founder of the Ferry, it was probably at the suggestion of his brother Robert the Augustine Monk, and grand masser of the Knights Hos- pitallers. This is the more presumable as several of the ferries for crossing the Mersey appear to have been established about that time ; and to have had Ecclesiastical origin. It is recorded that the ferry from Birkenhead to Liverpool was established by the Monks of the Benedictine Priory at Birkenhead, situate close to the water's edge, and known to this thy as Monk's Ferry ; whilst another was established between Eastham and Liverpool by the monks of St. Werbergs, Chester. Robert also seems to have obtained from his brother John, grants of land for the support of the Knights Hospitallers; but the Baron in his larger sympathy gave also a grant of land to the Order of Knights Tempters. These were given in "frank almoign,''a tenure by which a religious order hold lands to them and them successors for ever, on the eoqdition of offering up prayers regularly for the repose if the soul of the donor It seems more than a coincidence that on the suppres- sion of the Ord,:r of the Knights Tempters in the year 1309, a William de la More was the grand master of the Order in Eegland, suffering torture rather than accept liberty at the price of pleading guilty to false charges brought against the Order, and at last dying of a broken-heart in a dungeon in the Tower of London. Gareier de Naplouse probably in fulfilment of a promise made to RotHrt the master Hospitaller, by the second charter previously mentioned, made further provision for the maintenance of the ferry, and by the additional monetary grant also provided in accord with the religious faith of the time fel* the more efficient offering up of mama for the souls of the past and suc- cessive kith and kin of the Barons of Halton. Such appears to have been the somewha t singular circum- stances connected with the foundation of this " Ancient Ferry."

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
Letter from .a Warrington Policeman:

The following is a copy of a letter received by the Chief Constable from P.C. John Gibbs, at present serve ing with the 3rd Battalion Grenadier Guards in the Transvaal. P.C. Gibbs, who was a Guards reserveman, was called away from his duties ha the Police Force last August to rejoin his regiment at the front :—" Colliery Hill Camp, Belfast, Transvaal, October 2nd, 1900. Sir, —I trust you duly received the letter which I sent you from Capetown. After staying at that place two daye we entrained for Pretoria, breaking the journey at Bloom. fontein, where we stayed five days. We proceeded ots our way from there, in coal trucks, to Kroonstad where we remained one day and two nights, owing to the railway being blocked by a wrecked train. The partle culars of the wrecking you would doubtless have read its the papers. On the evening of the tenth day,atter leaving Capetown we arrived at Pretoria. We stayed one night only leaving early the following morning as escort to a convoy consisting of about 50 waggons and 5,003 oxen. Alter a march of eleven days we reached this place. On our way up country we passed 80419 notable placeo„such as Naauwpoort, De Aar, Colesharg, liens- burg, Roodeval, Balmoraldand many others, the names of which I forget. We are on outpost duty here, but do not know how soon we may be relieved or ordered to join our battalion. Our position is a healthy one, being on a hill about 5,000 feet above sea level. We have two nights to sleep and one night as advanced picket or guard. We are: under, canvas and find it a great treat after sleeping on the open veldt. The air at night ie terribly cold, with 18 to 20 degrees of frost every morn- ing. We have also heavy dews and thick fogs, but its the daytime groat heat. There is a rumour in camp that the battalion is picking up all small parties such as uel for the purpose of going home, but how true it is I can't say, for we get no news here about anything,nor have X receivea any letters from home yet, and don't think I: shall till we get back to Capetown. I shall not expect an answer to this letter as I may be on i:ny way home by the time you receive it.—l remain,sir,your obedient servant, J. Goes."

BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
A. FRIENDLY SOCIETY'S. SECRETARY IN TEE DOCK

T—he Warrington magistrates investieated a case on Monday, in which George Wagstaff, 102, Flarcly-street, wee charged with unlawfully withholding the sum of 25 3s Bd., the moneys of the United Operative Street Masons, Paviors and Stone Dresser' Society, on October 20th. He pleaded not guilty.— Mr Browne. who prosecuted on behalf of the seciety, observed that the case had been brought into court un- der the Friendly Societies' Act of 1875,by which defen- dants could be ordered to repay to the society all moneys received by him on behalf of that society, and d punish- ment could be inflicted for withholding such moneys. The society had a branch in Warrington, and was reels,- tered 776. The defendant was the local treasurer (De- fendant : And secretary), and he ought to have drawn he the money, and as a matter of fact did draw the sum of £5 34 81 which he oieeht to have tither paid into a bank or sent to the geueral secretary, Mr Maddricks. The branch got much into debt, the defendant did not pay what money be had received, many of the members owed money, and the result was that it was decided to dissolve the fecal society. This state of affairs was brought about by the negligence on the part of the defendant. The general secretary of the head office saw the defendant, who said , that he had lent the money out to different members.„ The secretary pointed out that he had no right to do anything of the kind, and that if he v.ould give the names of the members he would report the matter to the head office and see what could be done. The defendant, however, could not give the names, and then he asked to be allowed a week in which to pay the amount. There had been no dispute up to that time about the amount. The sum had been admitted in writing. After the week had passed a letter was received from the defendant to the effect that he had already in hand £2 17s 61. whigh ho had reflected, and promised to 'collect the full amount (25 3s 8d) by the end of the week He thanked Mr. Maddocks for his kindness in allowing the matter to be adjourned.— The Chairman: Has he appropriated the money to his own purposes ?—Mr. Browne : Ile has drawn it wile- ant the shadow of a tloubt, and it belongs to the head office. We want in order for the payment of the £5 3s 81. The money belongs to working men and not to too defendant. The defendant's duty was to hand over the money to the bank or to the treasurer. The treasurer has not received it and, therefore, it is owing.—?hilip Maddocks, general secretary of the society, then gave evidence in support of Mr. Browne's statemmt. He stated that it was in consequence of the terrible arrears of the local society, the head office decided to cancel it. He saw the defendant, and subeequeetly examined his books, and boned that he was £5 34 Si deficient. He asked him if that was aoeeed he said "Yes."—The Chair- man: Why did you riot require him to pay up week by week ?—Witness : The members are supposed to pay their contributions at the lodge, and the defendant enters them in the society's book and on the peece-card. He should have handed over all moneys to the treasurer.—The Chairman (to the defendant) : YOR have no more right av:ti the money than I hav:.. I don't think you real,z your position. What right have you to appropriate the money to your own use ? Defendant : I have not done so.—The Chairman : What has become of it ?-13=fendant : The members have it.—Mr Browne: He lied no right to give money back to-the m-mbera.—John H Themason, treasurer, said he tied received nothine from the defendant towards the peymeer. of the £5 3s Bd, which was still owiag.—Ser- geant Cheeney having given evidence, it was decided to order defendant to pay the mon-y within a week £5 3s 81—al! the court oosts, and the solicitor's fee, the alternative being a reonth's imprisonment.

ASSAULT 014 A RUNCORN CONSTADLR.—AzarIah Stephens. a seafaring man, was charged with being drunk and di.- orderly in High-street, on the 28th October. and further with assaulting P.C. Wilson whilst In the execution of his duty. The prisoner pleaded guilty.—P.C. Wilson stated that about 2.15 on Sunday afternoon he was on duty in Devonshire- square when he heard a disturbance in the direction of the Stanley Arms. On g sing there he saw the landlord and his son engaged in turning out a sailor. The landlord requested witness's assistance, and when they had got the man out the landlord, pointing to the prisoner. said " I want this mmn out as well as the other." Witness asked the prisoner to leave, but he refused and got hold of the partition. Witness had to use force to get him out, and when he was in the street prisoner became very violent Witness took hold of him by the arm, and told him if he did not go away quietly he would have to take him te the Police Station. He brought him some distance down the road, and prisoner struck out right and left, kicking witness on the side of th knee. Witness was bringing the other men along at the same time, but he had to release him in consequence of the prisoner's violent conduct. The prisoner wen, dawn on the road several times and " kicked and fought like a tiger" Mr. Ball came to witness's assistance, and they !got the handcuffs on, and Sergeant, Brewster by this time made his appearance. The prisoner. was drunk.—Mr. Harrison, landlord of the Stanley Arms.l said the prisoner and another man came into the house the worse for drink, and he declined to serve them. The prisoner was not so bad as the other man. He had to put the othq• man out. The prisoner never used a foul word to hint that he was aware of. The prisoner had ha I too much drink to be served.—Charies Ball, fruiterer. Nigh-street. cor- roborated al to assisting P.C. Wilson. He heard the disturb- ance in his house, and subsequently found the policeman and the prisoner in the channel nearly opposite Mr. Lake's office. The policeman's helmet was on the around. Witness held the man's hand while the handcuffs were put on. The prisoner was ve.y violent, and made several etteropts to kick Wilson.—Sergeant Brewster said the prisoner became very quiet when he saw him. He said witness was a gentleman, and he would come with him. Prisoner had had a bottle of whisky in his pocket, but !two smashed to atoms. He was a very respectable man when sober.—For the drunkenness prieor,er was fined 5s and costs, and for the assault 20s an costs.—The Chairman said they would allow Mr Bell 2s 6.1 for the services rendered to the officer. They commended Mr. Harrison for refusing to serve the men, and Mr. Ball for assisting the police.

Latchford v. Hale.

Hale visited Latchford on Saturday, and, as usual, a very interesting game ensued. From the start the game was very fast, and after some exchanges between the backs sale scored the first goal. Nothine, further was sewed before half-t although the home team did most pressing At tne re-start blth team; made deter- mined ends to score, and again the visitors notched the first point. Immediate!y afterwards Kertland netted the ball for the homesters. From the bull; -eff some more fast play folhwel. and Pearson secured the ball and equalised. Roth teams now played most vigorous'y,s,nd eventually Hale won by three goals to two. Stockton Heath v. Bowdon.

At Stock•on Heath on Saturday Bowdon played their strongest team. The home captain, the R4l? G W Dicisinst,n, was not available. Play opened very evenly from the bully. Bowdon taking things quietly for a while. The home defence was sound,and the forwards, by goed ccmbination,soon removed play to the Bowdon half, where the vialtore goalkeeper had to come out to clear. The Bowdon right wing made several praise- worthy efforts,which were not turned to account. After- wards Stockton Heath again pressed and almost scored. After the interval play ranged from end to end,and good work WR.II done on both sides. A very hard-fought game resalted in a draw, nothing being f clred.

div.head: Fire at Bewsey —Old Hall Farm,
div.p: Fire at Bewsey —Old Hall Farm,

Shortly before eight o'clock on Tuesday evenin g a fire was discovered iu a Dutch barn on Bewsey 014 Hall Farm, which id occupied by Mr. Arthur Hatton. The building contained four stacks of un- thrashed corn and a small stack of straw. The War- rington Fire Brigade, under the direction of Super- intendent Turner, were summoned, and were quickly on the scene with the steam engine Major. and assisted by an excellent supply of water from the adjoining pond they were not long in getting the flames (which on their arrival had obtained a firm hold of the whole of the stacks) under control. By ten o'clock the yard was in darkness, but it is feared that the whole of the stacks have been ren- dered quite useless. The loss is very serious, but it will we understand, be fully covered by insurance. This is the third lire which has occurred in this dis- trict within a fortnight, and the opinion is being expressed that there are one or two men going about wilfully setting fire to farm property. LANCASHIRE SENIOR COMPETITION.
Runcorn v. Warrington.

Some 3,500 persons were gather,d around the Irwdfl- lane arena, on Saturday last, witne,sing the contest bt- tween the above teams. Runcorn were minus Houghton, Warder and the two Butterworth, whilst Warrington had out a very representative team. Mr. Williams,Sal— ford, was the referee. The composition of the respective iiteens was as under _ _

Runcorn : Jolley, back; Stiaeley, Williamson, Wil- kinson and Jones, threequarters ; Richardson and Faulkner. halves; Walker, Lightfoot, Farmer, Reece, Gaycer. D rlington, Tomlinson and Dan, forwards. Warrington : Hallam, back; Fish, Isherwood. Dickin- son. and Hockenhatl, threequarters ; Bate and Burgess, halves ; Taylor, Morrison, Boardman, Mereweather, Eden, Antrobus. Swift, and Andrews, forwards Winning the toss Runcorn took advantage of the sun and wind, and Taylor no:hing daunted. landed the ball well into the Runcorn quarters where a scrimmage took place. Richardson ana Faulkaer effected an exchange out the latter was grassed before any advantage could accrue. Bate and Dickinson then took up the ruining and after a fine exchange gave Fish an opportunity from which a lot of ground was gained. Bate picked up I rem the heels of his forwards and transferred to Fish who ran in a try as the result of a capable effort. The try-getter failed to augment. From the restart Run- corn played up strongly, and Bate mulling a catch allowed several of the home forwaras to dribble to dangerous proximity of the Warrington goal. Hallam with careful and accurate judgment kept his charge free, and Bate gave relief with a punt. This agaia was fur tner improwd by Hoekenhall dribbling well into the Runcorn twente-five. Jolley replied. Warrington were coming again led by Taylor and Eden but an appeal for off- side returned to the centre. Several attempts were then made to cross the Warri ngton line, but Dickinson, Bur- gess, Fish and Hallam all took pars in a viaorous and effective defence. Faulkner had hard lines in not scor- ing falling short of the line by a few feet only. Runcorn continued to have the best of affairs, and though War- rington spurted away, Jolley returned with a smart run which might have been effective but for a slip at a criti- cal stage. Runcorn forwards and backs then passed well, but the wirepuller.' defence was too good for the Linnets. Burgess was subsequently injured and had to be carried off the field. Play had hardly been in pro- gress a minute when Jolley marked near the centre line. Hazardieg a kick the same player landed a magnificent goal. Runcorn were pressing but each side was visited in turn. Later play gravitated towards Flallam'a charge and Jones madetseveral capital attempts. At length the same player made an opportunity for Faulkner and that Mayer scored a surprieing try. Jolley failed at goal. Farmer marked in a good position but his kick at goal was indifferent. Burgess now returned. Following up a ruth Walker had bard lines in not being awarded a try. Runcorn continued to press and R.chardson picking up from a five-yards scrum scored a clever try. Shortly alter the interval came with:—Runcoro: 1 goal 2 tries,l 8 points; Warrington. 1 try. 3 points. Farmer re-opened the second half and was penalised. Play remained at centre for some time. Then be a series of kicks Runcorn found a foothold in the War- rington half. The stay was but a short one, however, as Isherwood and Fish got going and took the ball back. Joues re-:stablished the position by a succession of short dashes on the Runcorn right, but nothing tangible resulted. Bate at length gave Fish a chance on the left, and an exciting run resulted in his being carried into touch by Jolley and Williamson. Warring. ton then gained ground, and Stoneley was obliged to touch dead. From the drop out they attacked again but the defen ce was quite as capable, indeed, Jolle7 proved a resourceful back. Dickinson was the next to have a ehanee,but ha dropped the ball and sacrificed a certain try. It looked a alori-
THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, NOVEMBER 2, 1900.

one chance. Frrmo the drop-out, Runcorn forwards, Walker, Darlington and Lightfoot being conspicuous, took the ball back with a rush, and Faulkner, later. gave Farmer an opening. The bia man, however failed to cross the line. Reply'ng to lialam,Richardson dropped a goal. Then Warrington had a further sa.y in affairs, and Fish dropped beautifully, but a trifle short. Fol- lowing their advantage up Fish was given another chance, and made no bones about it. He dcdaed a c_Arple of fcrwards and was apparently going straight for Jolley, when that player beat forward to grasp him and he eluded him with a lieht bound, and scored one of the mcst delightful tries over witnessed at Runcorn. This too be improved with a pretty place-kick. From thence to the end both teams made efforts to improve their position but the finll result was ;—Runcorn two goals, two tries, 10 points ; Warrington, one goal, two tries, fight points.

The encount( r bet ween Warrington " A'' and Run corn " A " attracted a large number of spectators to the Wilderspool enclosure on Saturday. Warrington won the toss and took advantage of the wind. Shortly after the opening exchanges Runcorn invaded the War- ringtoa'l,alf, and scrimmages took place near the threi - quarter line. Duckworth made a mark and the homesters swooped down on th 3 visitors' goal. The Linnets were not caught napping however, and they made a fine defence. Injudic ous kicking by Ratcliffe resulted in one of the visitors' th:ee quar:ers making a mark and matters were transferred to the other end of the field. The home team succeeded in keaping the Runcorn men at bay and a passing movement between Lawless, Duck- worth and Harris.ended in toe latter player getting (-Nei.. The try was disallowed on account of a forward pass by Lawless. Ratcliffe mulled when a good opportunity presented irself• Warrington were allowed a free kick but Knight failed at goal, the ball passing just outside the posts. Ratcliffe go: the ball and (lodged his opponents but was grassed near the line. Offside OAF by Runcorn gave Knight another chance to kick a goal, but lie made a poor attempt. Runcorn dribbled into the Warrington territory and Moran made a capital run but was pulled up when very close to the line. War- rineturi played up briskly and nut Runcorn on the de- fensivo.Harris was gra.s,ed wh-n:within an ace of scoring Ratcliffe again distinguished h.m,eif, but half time arrived with ffrscore. On resuming both end s were visited in turn, bli.; nothing substantial aco.rued. Te result of the match was a pointless draw.

Boscow repel!ed the invasion, and an,thor fine run by KrOght folio wcu by some combined play between Ashurst and Scott saw the Engineers once more in the ascendency. Another sharp 'raid saw Werneth with a chance. but Boscow quickly recovered after maktiv, a mistake, and though Brady tried a drop at goal troin a difficait a ogle the interval arrived with the score shot blank. With the elements in their favour there was no doubt as to the issue of the match, for toe Enzineers settled to their work in business-tike style, and only a few minutes had elapsed when Barratt ! effected a fine run, and passing at the opportune moment to Timperley that player romped over the posts Ashurst placini the goal. div.head: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL. CREWE ALEXANDRA v. EARLESTOWN.
div.p: ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL. CREWE ALEXANDRA v. EARLES- TOWN.
Lancashire League.

At Cre we, before 2,C00 spectators. Lee started fo the visit ors, who at ortce got towards Coventry. Cun life relieved. and the game was transferred to Hales who got well down the home left, passing to Brookfield. This player made a good attempt to score. Hayes stop- ping his progress. Another raid by the home forwards resulted in the Earlestewn backs being beaten. Edgiry hit the post, but from the rebound Brookfield scored for Crewe. This success roused E trlestown, and some good work was witnessed from Pennington and Green in the half back division, Coventry saving in close quarters from Bartley. Lyon was next prominent with several good kicks, which were equally well taken by Hales time after time. This player came down to Earlestown fortress, but nothing except an unproductive corner followed. Similar favours to Earlestown, Hale was fouled but place kick failed. The visitors now exhibited some questionable tactics and were repeatedly pulled up for fouling. The free kicks, however, proved of no advantage, although Marshall missed easy chances from Breokfield, but the stubborn defence of Hall and Thcrepsen prevented any headway being made. The leather was kept in Earlestown line. where Marshall headed over twice. Chew afterwards was sorely pressed, but manag.ed to keep his goal clear. Half-time : Crewe 1, Earlestown nil. Final : Crews 4, Earlestown nil.

div.head: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.
TIIESDAY.—Before Hi Honour Judge Gwynne Jatncs,and Mr. J. D. Jollitre registrar.

ORDINARY BUSINESS.—The ordinary business of the Court wa:, taken up with 193 plaints ; 3 defaults ; and 43 judgment summonses. MINOR CASES.—John Leather Stellfox, assignee of Dr M. McKenzie, Runcorn, sued Joseph Grindley. Surrey.. street, successfully for £1 133.—John William Dockery, music teacher, Rumlorn, sued Thomas Ashcroft, E later, Waterlco-road for 103 6d.—8!3 Honour, however, hav- ing decided on the merits of the case, gave judgimeat for plaintiff for 75 6d.

HIS Bosom-3 ADVISES THE BUTCHER.—In a case of Watson and Sons, butchers, Church btreet, Fredsham, versus Hayes Frodsham, the former claimed 22s 4i for meat supplied.—Mr H N Linaker (Messrs Linaker and Linaker) defenceed.— Plaintiff subitantiated his claim from which it appeared the only item in dispute was a shoulder of lamb supplied to the defendant on the 4th of Auetist.—The defence was that Mr Hayes had tendered 183 M in payment of the bill, but wored not pay for the shoulder of lamb in dispute.-9 little girl gave evidence as to delivering the shoulder on August 4th and stated she remembered the occasicn for she had written the date down cn a piece of paper in her bedroom. Defendant admitted the shoulder had been brought to the house, but was sent back be- cause it was not ixactly the weight she had ordered.— His Honour in giving judgment, said the girl's story was , a most extraoruinary one, and he could not eive any credence to it. Judgment for plaintiff for 183 911 tt.e amount tendered.—Watson and Sons, then sued Mr Lister of Frodsham Bridge, for an amount due for meat.—Questioned by his Honour as to who gave the order tor them. Plaintiff said he did not know. The order was received and the goods were delivered,-11- fendant swore ho gave no orders to tbe plaintiff or to his housekeeper to deal with the defendant.—His Honour in giving ju dement fcr the defendant, advised Watson next time he had a case of that nature to consult a solicitor. The way some cases were brought before him showed that the plaintiffs were really ignorant as to what was evidence or not. THE GIRL, ATTIE YOUTH, AND TRH MARBLE SLAB,— Thomas Atherton, chip potata merchant, Frowliam, sued Mary Lockett, a single woman, Church-street, Frodsham, for 5s 61:1 damages coused by the breaking of a scab -lab..—lt appeared the girl Leckett met a youth earning out of Atherton's crtablishment, whom she knew. For a lark she plucked his favour out of his coat, and also took his cap off. There was a bit of frolic and the slab on the scales was knocked over and smashed.— Defendant thought that because it was an accident she was not liable. His Honour, however, disabusad ber of this idea, and gave judgment far the amount claimed.- -Defendant said she lived at home and could not pay. —Elia Honour : If you go larking about in this way you must pay for the damage. Order for 23 a month.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

THE REV. J. A. WHlTLEY.—Readers will be pleased to hear that the Rev J A Whitley, sOLI of Mr JAMES Whit- ley, drocer, of Stockton Heath, has finished his term at Yale Divinity College, U.S.A., has graduated M.A..8.D., and has been appointed minister of the Wesleyan Church at Pennycook, Conn. Mr. Whitley worked his passage out to Canada when a boy, and was employed there as a labourer. Be saved a litre money, and studied at a small school in the United States. Here he gained scholarships, and passed free to a higher Fchoot. He was most successful, and finally won a scholarship which enabled him to a,o to Yale Divinity College. At that institu.ion he gained many valuable prizes. AN OBJECT4II TO VACCINATION —Arthur Newton, who resides at 7, Gaskell-street, Stockton Beath, applied to Megsrs. Yr. Long (in the chair) and F. A. Frost, the ma- gistrates sitting at the Dare sbury Petty Sessions on Tuoaday, for a certific tte exempting his child from vac- cination. He said that about four or five years ago he had a child which was in very good health until it was vaccinated, when it was attacked by eczema and died. Be firmly believed that its death was due to the effects of vaccination.—The Clerk : Did the dcctor certify that the eczema was cawed by examination P—Appli. cant: You could not get a doctor to say such a thing. —The Clerk : Be might have told you what he thought the cause of death was.— Applicant Yes, but they ' don't tell you what you want to know. In answer to the Chairman, he said the child was vaccinated by a private dootor. —The Chairman said applicant took a great responsibility upon himself in not having his child vaccioated.—Applicant : After considering the matter I have come to the conclusion that I would sooner have an exemption certificate.—The Chairman said they could not refuse, and granted the application.
The English Draughts Association.—lmportant
Alte-ration of Rules.

The annual general meettag of the English Draughts Association was held last Saturday at the Sultan Café, Cheapside, Lou ion, F.C, the president, Mr AV Carruthers, in the chair. The following clubs and individual members were represented :—J Stephens (hon. president), W Carruthers (president), (1 A Oelsthorp (treasurer), R Atwell (secretary), W Bell (Hanley), It H Davies (Liverpool), F Dunne (Warrington), TJ Riley (Nottingham), B Woolhouse (London), J K Lyons (Liverpool), T Townsend (Littleborough), A Hynd (Manchester), 11. Borlflsh (Birmingham), Leeds City D.C., Leeds D. and C.C., North End D.J. (Liverpool), Nottingham D.C., Warrington Draughts League, Warrington C and D.C. London D.C., Manchester Central DC., London Wanderers D.O„ and Birmingham DX: Officers for the ensuing year were elected, the only changes being that Mr W J Wray (Halifax) was appointed secretary in place of Mr R Atwell (London), who resigned, and Mr J K Lyons was elected auditor in place of Mr Vray. There was considerable discus- sion over a number of proposed alteration of the rules. In the result, Mr Stephens's proposition that the championship tourney should be held annually (instead of biennially, as at present) was negatived as was also )Jr A Hynd's proposal to abolish the new time rule, introduced at the last meeting of the association.

CONSTIPATION.

This is a disease which may be looked upon as the mainspring of more than half the ills which afflict mankind. It consists of an irregular and insufficient action of the bowels, and its commonness is remarkable, especially among women. Though there are other causes of constipation, the principal one is an irregularity of habit in attending to the laws of nature. Insufficient liver action will also produce it. Constipation is not so exttemely difficult to cure as many people imagine. A few doses of BILE BEANS, taken as directed, will effectually remove the present trouble, and if strict regularity of habit in effecting or endeavouring to effect an evacug- tion be joined to a course of the BEANS, constipation will not be found to recur.
LOCAL BANKRUPTCY CASE. A Settlement Declared Void.

Before His Honour Judge Gwynne James, at the War- rington County Court, last Thursday, in the case ot William Johnson Johnson, of the Mount, Penketh, gentleman, bankrupt, a motion was made by the Official Receiver (Mr C J Dibb) and trustee of the property of the bankrupt for an order declaring an indenture of settlement dated the Ist day of December, 1893, and m tele between the baskrupton the one part and Ttionias Atthur Matthews, R',bert Edwin Mattnews, and John Wilkinson of the other part, to be declared fraudulent and void aq against the creditors of the bankrupt, and that the property comprised therein vest in the said C. J. Dibb.

Mr. Acton (instructed by Messrs H B White and Sons) made the appl,cation on behalf of the Official Receiver. Mr Hogg (instructed by Meisrs Jeans and Son) appeared fqr the trustees of the settlement, and Mr W J Forahave appeared for the bankrupt. The case was argued at considerable length by the learned counsel.

IHis Honour, in giving judgment, said this was a motion brought before him in the bankruptcy of Mr W J Jehasen on behalf of the Official Ii c aver asking him to set aside a voluntary settlement made by the bank- rupt on September 1, 1893. Mr Johnson was adjudicated bankrupt on June Les of the present year. He (his Honour) found the following facts : The bankrupt came of age on the 21st of August, 1893, and on the Ist of September of the same year he entered into a voluntary agreement dealing wish certain property. The property in question was conveyed to trustees, three et whom were Mr Johnson's uncles, under certain trusts, mae of them beino that in the case of his bankruarcy he woe to be deprived of this property and to have no control over it. The trustee in bankruptcy asked him ,(nis Honour) to say that owing to that clause in the case of bankruptcy, the bankrupt's interest in the estate should ceise, and that the settlement was void as against the creditors in the present bankruptcy.. Three grounds were suggested upon which be (his Honour), should find the settlement was void. The first was under section 47 of the Bankruptcy Act, and in order that the wettlemcnt might be void within the meaning of that section for the purpose of the present case he (his Honour), must be satisfied. it was a volun- tary settlement made within ten years of the bankruptcy and at the time the settlement was made the bankrupt was insolvent. Now undoubtedly it was made within ten years of the present application, but whether the bankrupt was solvent or not was a questicn which he had to determine. Apart from the :property dealt with, which it was sought to set aside, and which came to the bankrupt under his grandfather's will through his mother, he was also entitled to property under his father's will., his father having died in January, 1891. He (his Honour), would not go into details as regarded the contents of that will, but it appeared that the bankrupt and also, he snould think, the trustee a under the will were in doubt as to the position of the bankrupt and obtained a declaration subsequently in court to determine what his real interest was. The Court of Chancery decided that he was absolutely entitled under his father's will to a ruin of over £4,000. . Taking that interpretation of the will, which, of mfrs.., he (his Honour) must take and which he did, it appeared that ea the time of the voluntary settlement of September, 1893, the hankrapt was entitled to absolute possession of over £4,000 under his father's will. It was not suggested that the bank- rupt at that time had debts anything approaching that extent. It was, however, suggested that he did not know he was entitled to that amount, but whether he knew it or not, he certainly had in his (the Judge's) opinion a valuable asset which more than covered the amount of the existing debts at the time of the settlement. Trit; disposed of the first questioo, namely, whether at the time of the settlement h.? wee insolvent. Another point taken was thet this settlement was void under common law on the ereteed that this was a young man who was improper!e induced on coming of ago to sign this settlement under the forcible arguments of his re- lations. Be (his Honour) thought that argument entirely failed. He had read the afli iavit of the trwtees, and eflaeciallv the affidavit of one of the bankrupt's uncles, Mr R E E Matthews, who read the settlement to this young man and thor6ughly ex- plained it to him and he (his Bonoor) had not the slightee; doubt that the bankrupt thoronely uedersteed it. and at the ssme time Mr Matthews who was his aolicier and knew the importance of it, said he was particulArly careful in so doing. There was not the shadow of evidence to support the Official:Receiver or set wide a document of this kind on a suggestion Viet 'there was ant' endue pres=ure put upon the settler. That beine so he (nig Honour), came to the last ground on which he -eaa asked to sot it aside, namely under statute 13 Elizabeth, eaapter 51 but he was*ask"d to set aside under that statute on the ground that the object of the settlement was to defeat and delay creditors. The Cases which had been quoted in support laid down in general terns the proposition that a voluntary settlement by anyoneo which contained a clause transforeng his property was void as against the trustee in bankreptcy should he feibscealently become bankrupt. It had been contended on behalf of the trustees that this case did not applo be- cans' in the present instance the valor was solvent a' the time be entered into the voluntary settlement in 1893. Counsel admitted that he could cite no cases forl the segeestion made, namely that if the settler wag sol- vent when he entered into the agreement that the clatlFe transferring his pronerty be settlement was a roestian for the judge. Whether that he so or net he would pre- sume for the aeke of areument that it was for him (his Ffemour) to settle, although he was strongly of epireinn legally that he should be oblieed to say it was void apart from any evidence. He was of opinion that the object of this settlement was to protect the settler against himself and to protect him from c-editors. But the object of the trustees was, in his (the Judge's) npinion, a perfectly legitimate ebjsct in this sense that they did not think they were doing wrong at the time they induced Joansan to enter into the' settlement. On calming of rev here was this youne man £7OO in debt. It wae admitted that he was a spendthrift. Within a very short time afterwards he had caper, all that came to him under his father's will,seme £4,000,

and these trustees no doubt put their heads together and s4id " now we will see if we cannot take some steps for this young gentleman so that he will not be able to squander it all away." The settlement was therefore agrePd upin. The trustees had act-el perfectly bona-fide throuzhout, and acted on the interests eairely ot the settler, but no doubt from a point of law they had gone tOo far. He declared that the trustees of the settlement should pay to the Official Receiver as he should trom time to time certify a sufficient sum to pay al: the debtors debts and costs, fees and percentages to and in- cidental to the bankrupt, the costs of all parties to come out OE the settlement.

div.head: MR. F. MONKS AND THE CORPORATION.
div.p: MR. F. MONKS AND THE CORPORATION.
Celebration Dinner at the Town Hall,

In honour of Warrington attaining the additional power and dignity of a County Borough, Mr F Monks JP., who has been one of the represehta- tives of Warrington on he Lancashire County Council since the creation of that authority, but whose duties will, of course, now cease in conse- quence of the powers which Warrington has ob- tained as a County Borough, entertained the mem- bers of the Corporation and officials and a few in- vited guests at dinnerat the Town Hall,last evening This new era in the municipal life ot the borough. has therefore been doubly celebrated at two sump- tuous banquets. There were present in addition to the host, the Mayor (Alderman Roberts), the Mayor's Chaplain (Rev J l'onge). Alder- men Fairclough (deputy-mayor), Franc-m:2h, Green, Heaton, Hutchinson, Councillors BAird Bennett, Barton, Duncan, Davies, Ellison, Johß Evans, James Evans, Forshaw, Greening, A Jolley, A J Jolley, Monks, Malkin, Peacock, Pierpoint, Pie mnton, F R Robert., John Roberts. togere, Smethurst, Tinnion, Wilkinson, Messrs J Lyon Whittle (town clerk), T Longdin (borough sur- veyor), J Fairhurst (borough treasurer), G F F White (deputy magistrates' cterk), J Dens (water engineer), W S Haddock (gas engineer), F Taylor (secretary gee department). Dr Sout (notice sur- geon), C Madeley (librarian), R G Henshall, W Fletcher (Whitley). William Owen, Seger Owen, Nelson Jackson, and the editors of the local papers. The guests assembled in the large committee rota and afterwards walked in procession to the Chamber where the dinner was served. ?Lents and flowers had been freely used in the decoration of the building and the whole presented a pleasing ensemble. During dinner, Mr It El Pearson" orchestra discoursed swear music. At the conclusion of the repast, a num- ber of tosste were proposed and duly honoured. One of the most interesting events of tho AVeriins! was the or-- sentation of an illuminated card to Mr F Monks, J P., Alderman Francornb and Councillor Pterp)int,recording the resolution of thanks passed by the Council acknowledging the services of these three gee- tlernen on the Lancashire County Council as representatives a Warrington. Each card had been tastefully designed and was embellished with a portrait of the Mayor. The toast list was egret- ably interspersed with humorous recitals by Mr. Nelson Jackson, selections by the orchestra, and glees by Vie Orpheus Glee Party, consisting of Messrs Davenport, Whitehouse. Sherlock, and Scattergood. Toe catering of Mr. Powys gave every satisfaction. Toe usual local :oasts were briefly proposed by the Cuarnmeat (Mr F and drunk with musical honoors.

The toast of the Mayor, members of the Council and officials, was next proposod by the CFULIR'IIad. tie re- called the faet tnat he accompanied his father whets be went to record his vote,in the election for the first mem- br.rs of the Warrington Town Council. At the time he , was only 12 or 13 years of age but he re- membered the ioterest taken in that event. He had switched the growth of the Corperation from its birth and he thouzht he might fairly claim that he had done a fair share of the work—(hear, hear)—and that he was entitled to the rest which he was now takiu,g. (Hear. bear.) Ile was very that fol to say that although he was not a member of the Corporation laimielf, his son— applause—was doing hi duty with the rest of the Coun- cil in carrying on thework of the C3rporation (flear.hear) Referring to the exullent manner in which the Mayor discharged his duties, he said be represented in his co.- borate capacity all toe virtues of the Corporation, and had fulfilled the dutiei of the office to the 6atisfaction of ~veryone. (Hear. hear.) He understood that the Mayor was to bl elected for a second year, and therefore he would be the first Mayor Of the Cousity Borough of Warrington. (Hear, hear). If the duties were discharged with the game ability.and success as had been the case this year they would have reason to congratulate themselves. Doring the year of his office he had taken the initiative in many reforms which lal been for the benefit of the town. (Hear, hear.) From persons outside the Council he had beard expressions of approval of the work done by the Cor- poration. So far as they might be permitted to trespa-s 'iii the domain of private life' he thought tLey could also cemmend the services of theMayoress—(applause)—ind the capable manner in which she had assisted bee hn- hand in his Mayoral duties. (Applause.) The MaYOR, in responding, said he was sure they would pardon him if he acknowledged in the first place, in very grateful terms, the manner in which the Chair- man bad refa.red to his wife. Be could say with all honesty that he had received everything which loyal devotion on the part of a wife to her husband, could give, in discharging his public duties dur- ing the first year of his mayoralty. He should have very great pleasure in conveying to her the kind expres- sions made, of the way in which she had done her duty. The Mayor proceeded to refer to the 27 years of his public life and to the:assistance he received at the begin- ning of his career from Mr Monks and other gentlemen. INerring to the duties which devclved upon members

of:-.hesCarporation be said there was no connection be- tween Imperial politics and municipal administration and tne more thoroughly the two political parties recognised this fact the better it would be for the Town in the future. (Hear, hear.) Speaking of his Mayoral duties, the Mayor said be had neither spared his health nor strength and be hoped he had at any rate deserved what he had received and that was the cordial support and approbation of the great majority of hie fellow townsmen. (Hear, hear.) It was, of course, impossible to please everybody and yesterday he was afraid be disappointed or dissatisfied at least two or three aspiring individuals for honours in the Town Council. He could assure them that it was not a pleasant duty but at the same time he had no option in the matter and was compelled to carry out the advice given by the Town Clerk. (Hear, hear.) He wished to say as a warning that his experieacea of yesterday revealed an amount of improper conduct on the part of some persons connec- ted with the nominations submitted to ,him, which he did not believe had ever been equalled in the history of this town. (Hear, hear.) It might come to be a matter of necessity to use whatever power the law permitted to prevent a repetition of what was most disgraceful to all concerned. He hoped such another experience would not occur dur- ing his Mayoralty. In justice to the fact that all the papers he was called upon to examine were invalid be felt bound to give common warning that if those responsible would not carry out what the law required they must be prepared to accept the censequences. In cuncluiioo, he stated that the future of our town promised to be a very bright one indeed and he believed that Warrington in a few years would have a population of nearly one hundred thousand. (Applause.) The MAYOR, later in the evening, presented the illu- minated earth to the ex-county councillora, who in- dividually acknowledued the compliment.
