div.head: AN ILLEGAL: DISTRAINT. Case at the Warrington County
div.p: AN ILLEGAL: DISTRAINT. Case at the Warrington County
Court.

At the Warrington County Courtlast Thursday, Edward Nunneries?, a signal man on the Cheaaire Lines railway, residing at 2, Warrington-view, Latchford, sued his brother-in-'aw,Johnßichardson for damages for an illegal distraint. Mr. Acton, barrister (instructed by Mr For- shaw) represented the plaintiff and Mr A Browne ap- peared for the defendant, who put in a counter claim for five weeks rent, amounting to £1 73 61, which he alleged was due to him from the plaintiff.—Mr Acton stated that in 1891, the plaintiff's father-in-law ee,cupied the lease of some land at Walton and the plaintiff entered into an arrangement with him to build two cottares on tha land. Accordingly he bought some farm buildings for £3O, which be pulled down and used the building material in the erection of two cettayaa on the and. The plaintiff bad paid something like £BO towards the cost of erecting the cottages and had also lived on the premises himself for a considerable period. The plaintiff resided in one of the cottages and hi father-ii.-law lived in the other from 1891 to July 1899. In July 1899 the plaintiff sold tne cottages by auction and they were bought by the defendant John Richardson. On the 14th of August Richardson called at the plaintiff's house and brought a tent buok with him and claimed rent at the rate of 5s 6d a week. Plaintiff refused to vay it and on the 25. h August a letter was written by Mr Browne demanding payment Pif 11s for two week's rent. No agreement hid been entered into between the parties as ti what rent should be paid. and ,naturally the plaintiff refused to pay it. On the 26:h Decemb-n., Mr Gittens, who was a certified bailiff, entered the plaintlff'3 premises and levied a distraint for £1 13s 01, which was said to be for six weeks' rent, and 73 61 his fee. Plaintiff paid the money under nrotest and now came before the court and asked for damages for what he (Mr Acton) submitted was an iileal distraint.— Plaintiff was called and here out the above statement. In cross-examination by Mr Browne witness admitted that his wife told him that she believed his brother-in- law had bought the property. Be denied that he tv,r agreed to pay the rent. Mr Richardson asked for 5s 6d per week and he said he would pay 5,, which Richard- son would not mccept.—Mr lkowne called the defendant who stated that he fold his brother-in-7asv when he bought the property, and informed him that if be wished to remain in the Pottage he must pay 54 6.1 a week. Plaintiff offered him 53. Mr Browne contended that the Waintiff was a tenant at will at the time of the pur- chase of the property bythe defendant andwas therefore liable for rent.—Toe judge said he did not think plaintiff was a tenant at will, as from the statement which had been submitted it was shown that he paid his father 41 a week for rent. His Honour also held that there was no agreement betwe.en the parties ler the payment of rent, and therefore an illegal distraint had been com- mitted. He give judgment for the plaintiff for £1 datnaea and costs. He also gave judgment for the plaintiff on the counter-claim, but suggested that in order to prevent any future litigation, the plaintiff should pay 54 a week for the five weeks claimed.

A Warrington Man Hangs Himself. James Lee, a herb beer manufacturer, residing at 64, Hardy-street, committed suicide on Saturday by hanging himself. It appears that he had had no less than three attacks of influenza during the pre- sent year, the last one occurring some few weeks ago. In consequence he had been in a despondent state of mind, but had never threatened to do away with himself. At 5.40 on Saturday morning his wife got up and went to work at the factory, leaving her husband in bed. Se returned at 1.15 in the afternoon and found the deceased hanging by a rope from a post which supported a partition in the kitchen. She had the presence of mind to cut him down and sent for the police P.C. Clough came upon the scene hut on his arrival, life was extinct. At the inquest, which was conducted at the Police Station on Monday afternoon, by Mr F A Jones, the deputy clroner, a verdict of " Suicid e whilst of unsound mind " wa3 returned.

div.head: Letter to the OTittor.
div.p: Letter to the OTittor.
A Defence of "Ignorant Runcorn.'

Sir,—On behalf of the residents of Runcorn I must enter my protest against Canon Wood's remarks made at the opening of St. Michael's Bazaar. I refer to what be says about us being poor, ignorant, etc. In the first place if we are all Canon Wood says we are, I question his taste in saying it, but I think Canon Wood does not know the people of Runcorn sufficiently to speak on their behalf. The only people that he can claim to know are his own particular sect, and I should like to have the private opinion of a few of his prominentsupporters, at election and other times, as to how they like being styled poor and ignorant. What do the lawyers and doctors of the town say about it? I have always looked up to them in the past, but I suppose now I must drag them down to my own level. What about the member of the School Board who told us after the School Board Election " that his father had not left him money, but had left him brains" how does be like being called ignorant ? When the Canon spoke of the people being poor he was evidently gauging them by the amount of the collections in his own places of worship. I cannot imagine what other chance he has of knowing the finan- cial position of the people, but I think this was arguing from the particular to the general which the Canon once told the members of the School Board was bad logic. To show the badness of his logic I would remind him of the fact that another sect in the town has during the last two years raised over £3,000 for Church purposes, in addition to the ordinary expenditure, without the aid of bazaars. They at any rate are not poor' or if poor, very generous. As to l.eing ignorant we have not all had the opportunities and advantages which the Canon had of having a University education, but I think most of us would have bad better manners than he. a Master of Arts, had, and would not have thrown it in the teeth of his more unfortunate fellow townspeople that they 'were ignorant. The people of Runcorn are getting heartily sick of Canton Wood's assumed intellectual and financial superiority.—Yours etc.,

div.head: TEAM.
div.p: TEAM.
Annual Distribution of Prizes.
Speech by Mr. A. H. Crosfield.
Councillor Pierpoint and the Recent
Election.

The annual distribution of prizes, generously pre- sented by the President (Mr. Arthur H. Crosfield), to members of the bowling team took place in the Liberal Club, Warrington, on Saturday evening. At six o'clock a capital tea was partaken of by a large gathering and subsequently a " social " was held in the reading-room. Mr. A. H. Crosfield occupied the chair and the attendance in- cluded, Councillors Pierpoint,Tinnion, Peacock, F R Roberts, William Roberts; Drs. Smith and Kisby, and Messrs Pemberton (secretary), G F Freeman (joint secretary) T. Critchley (Chairman of the Bowling Green Committee), T Locker (captain), Daintith (sub-captain), W Furness, John Harrison and Lamb (manager of the club.) The loyal toasts were honoured on the proposition of the Chairman. An interesting programme of songs. etc., was then submitted. The vocalists were Messrs W Critchley, H Price, J D Brimelow, and J E Warren, and their cent ri bastions save every satisfaction. A humorous recitation by Mr E A Sanders created much laughter, and an oboe solo "The lost chord" by Mr F Davies was effleiently rendered. Mr T P Ford, who accompanied, deli ghted the assembly with solos on the concertina and the pianoforte, and Mr Whittaker was very successsful with a whistling solo. Particular mention must be made of a patriotic song which was sung by Mr Brimelow. The words had been written by Mr J E Warren, and the music was composed by Mr Ford, and needless to say this item met with a hearty reception, rho chorua was spiritedly suns by all present. Couecillor PIERPOINT, in proposing the toast of the " Bowling Team? expressed his pleasure at finding himself once again in Bewsey-street. It was a matter of profound regret to him that he was unable to take part in the past election, which was fought so admirably by his friend the Cnairman. But his position was that he had as it were laid down the active part of his work for Liberalima in Warrington, feeling that he was entitled to take a share of rest ' and give up to sum's considerable extent the work which he had undertaken for so many years for this great party. He did not know that ever he passed over a day of the election without feeling very much like a fish out of water, but having made up his mind that it was his duty to himself Co remain as it were, quiescent, except in the matter of the voting, and having declared previously that he weuld not take part in any election in Warrineton,he felt he was bound to stick to his word. He was not going to reproach them for forcing an eleetion and he was net going to find fault with those active members of the party who thought it was otting and meet that this borough should be fought. Soe.aking personally, he was sorry they had an election. fie could only see one end of it—the end that was ob- tained at the finish and from his point of view he could not see that any weed was obtained by fighting the elec- tion. He was sorry the Liberal party was placed in the pesition it was on the night of the election. He was exceedingly sorry for Mr Crostield. A better man at a candidate they never had—(applause)—and he regretted that he had not tad an opportunity of showing his true value, because four days were not enough—four weeks were not enough to win an election. They proved that in the course of the last election. Mr Scott had fourteen days to carry on the contest but evea in that space of time they found it was absolutely imeos- sible to canvas the whole of the borough. It was no use' ~ighting an election in this town or any other unless they were prepared to do the work of hcuse to house canvassing. If they could not do that the result was bound to so against them. At all events they bad in Mr. Crosfield a good candidate, a man who in his (the speaker's) opinion was absolutely sound on all Liberal principles. As he grew older he would grow mellower and more in touch with the great democracy of this country. Ho was hardly the democrat that he (the speaker) would Ilk to see him because he was afraid that Mr Crosfield was touched with what he (Mr Pierpoiat) considered was a very great crime on the part of a large number of the Liberal party—the so called Imperialism. They would have enough of Imperialism before they had finished with it and 60/119 of them would be exceedingly Berry that they ever put their hands co such a dirty brush. They entieipated very great good from it : but he (Mr. Pierpoint) saw vary much harm. He thoueht Imperialism Was an invention of the devil and was of no good to anyone. In propos- ing the toast he referred to the progress of the bowling team and said that in the present captain—Mr. Thomas Locker they had an experienced bewler,whose example would be of valise to the younger members of the club to keep the game on that hiete place which they all so much desired to see. (Applause.) A great many people said it Naas a pity that bowling greens were attached to public houses. Unfortunately if a man was fond of the game and be could only go to the green which was attached to a public house they could not blame him. He WAS very pleased indeed to see some remarks which were reported in the press, advocating a municipal bowling green for Warrington. They had a municipal bowling green in the town of Macclesfield and it was very much anpreciated by workingmen. He did not see why the Corporation of Warrington should not 'take the matter in hand. The green should not be in opposition to any existing green but should only afford an opportunity for thoee men who did not belong to any club and who did not cars to so to a public house green, to indulge in the game. He bad very great pleasure in proposing the "bowling green team" coup- ling with it the LIAM of the captain, Mr TiI3MAS Locker.

Toe toast was heartily honoured. Mr. A. H. CM:WIELD, who bad a cordial reception, said he had not intended to speak upon podtics that night but he must thank Mr Pierpoint for the vary in- teresting opinions he-had given them upon the recent political contest in the town. He also thanked Mr Pier- point very much indeed for the kind opinions he bad expressed about bins (Mr Crosfiald). He (Mr Crosfield) hoped he had not got the foolish tancy to imagine that he was as experienced or capable a polilcian as they could have to fight their battles, and if he were not go- ing beyond the subject he would like everyone to clearly understand that if they in the future got a more experiecced and capable politician than himself to fight their battlee be was prepared to be wit'n them and fight for him. He should think it a great piece of presump- tion and impertinence to in any way seem to foist him- self or force himself upon them after having had this conteet. On the other hand, he could tell them from the bottom of his heart that it was the greatest possible honour to be allowed to fight as their candidate at the recent election. (Applause.) He could assure them that as regarded the majority against him, that did not worry him at all. (Ls welater.) No, he thought of the 3,303 friends of the old cause who at a critical time, with everything against them, showed their constancy and fidelity to principle and stuck to the ship. To have been permitted te fight their battle was an lionoue he should never forget. (Cheers.) Sympa- thetic friends seemed to expect to find one smashed, demolished and pulverised—(laughter)—but they were very wide of the mark. (Hear, hear.) There was nothing to be ashamed of in fighting for a gool cause and he felt proud of the support, the enthusiastic and more than friendly support they had all given to him. (Applause.) That was a pleisent thing to reflect ore, and there had been many pieasant features in this cont,sh For one thing, there had been none of that acrimonious recrimination—(laughter)—an expression which he believed Mr. McMinnies once coined no ill- natursd feult-fin,ling and uphrailing over the defeat. They ihcognised mistakes and shortcomings. only that they might repair them. (Hear, hear ) From their apponents lee had received the greatest cnurtesy, and as regarded their member, Mr. Robert Pierpoint and he were jest as good friends as ever they were, or, if be might enderso his remark, still teetter friends as they came more in contact with each other. (Hear, hear.) Well these were pleasant relations, and he hoped end believed they would not be impaired by the harder hitting that might be in store for both, of them in the future—(beer, hear)—because close fighting did gener- ally lead to hard hitting, and close fighting in the future he ventured to predict there would be Mr William Pierpoint had discussed the criestion whether they were wise and whether it was expedient to have a contest ; but they must not throw the responsibility on Ills shoulders. Some months ago they discussed the mareer, and he told them then that if they wanted him to fi;bt he was there, and he should say, if they asked him, exactly the same next time.2.(Leud applause). So long as they wanted him he would do, as he did last time, his level best, and fight as earnestly and sincerely as he knew how. (Applause). At the last election he tried to keep clear of what he hated and detested in politics, and that was clap-trap and bunkum. There was not a thing in his modest election address, and not a reform discussed during their very brief conte;t that he would not have striven to advocate to the best of his ability if he had been returned to Parliament. In fact, he tried to be on the cautious Mho and he would have gone further and done more. (Hear, bear.) His friends had teld him this was not an occasion for an election spteeti and he believed be had done his fair share of speaking recently. (Laughter.) He did, however, just want to say can word more. They sometimes heard it laid that the Liberal Party had exhausted its mandate, that they were played out. The wish was father to the thoeght. (Laughter.) One of the last utterances of their ereatest chief was the remark that the first part of Liberal work was in a fair way to be accomplished.

and he would he a shallow individual indeed who would seek to under-rate the vast significance of that work. Emancipation, civil and religious, political and cum- merciel, what a blessing it had been to the whole nation; both to Britain at home and to greater Britain beyond the seas. The second half of their task would bring ereeter blessings still. (Hear, hear.) This constructive work might be more difficult, but, if possible, it was even more important than the work of emancipation which had gone before.He Was not going to detain them by discussing in detail what that programme meant. but let them just consider a few of the reforms the Liberal party had yet to carry. There was first of all, temperance reform; reform he took it, on the lines of Lord Peel's report, something that was feasible anS practicable. Then they had the great question of the housing of the poor referred to in such an admirable speech from a man who had given much thought to the subject, last night. (Hear, hear). Then from the same quarter they looked for great things in the way of reform at our War Office ; reforms carried out not in the interests of a few, but in the interests of the whole community and Empire. Then they heard in 1895 a great deal about Old Age Pensions. Whenever it came to be their turn to take up that question, he ventured to say the Liberal party would deal with it as he thought they had dealt always with great measures of reform on their merits, and not merely as a methed of Yrne-catching, or as something to be taken up just !Ames election and dropped after it. Another great economic measure, and one affecting the interests of every ratepayer in our town and other towns wag taxation of Ground Rents, (Hear, hear.) He only gave them a bare recital of these reforms, hut just consider what they meant, how they would influence and affect the well-being of the whole community land the happiness ref their homes and families. If they considered the matter he thought they would have a very gaol answer to those who told them that the Liberal programme had been exhausted. (Hear, hear.) They in Warrington ought to have some share in this work—(hear, hear)—and he therefore urged them to continue to give their best support with patience and courage, with prudence and with energy to those principles and those measures which, to again quote their old friend, Mr McMinnies, "have made the fame of statesmen and the glory of the Nation." (Applause) He was not going to try to controvert what Mr William Pierpeint had said as to the expediency or in- expediency of having the recent eleetion, but he thoueht it had at least this salutary effect that it was educational—(hear, heart—end what they wanted in this constituency was 'education. (Hear, hear.) BF- tweet' now and the next figh- a great deal of work had got to be done. So far as he was concerned he could only tell them this, that with regard to the sinews of war, he , could only say that he would cheerfully fork out— (laughter)—as much as he could afford in furthering the Liberal cause in Warrington. (Applause.) That, he could assure them be would do con amore Ile did not grudge what it had cost him in the recent contest, which, under the circumstances, was a very 'satisfactory battle Indeed. (Hear, hear.) But when all was said and done, the issue of the future rested with them- selves, apd it was for them to consider whether the Cause they were fighting for deserved that petience.pru- deuce and energy by which the' could if they chose re- peat once more the glorious victory of 1880. (Cheers.) There was just now a great deal of Imperialism in the air, and this last week Some high-flown, if not really eloquent remarks had been made about it, remarks all the same which would have come with more propriety and a truer ring from the lips of some one, who had not just been engaged in exploiting patriotism for party Purposes. (Hear, hear.) Well, they as Liberals thought they were just as good friends of their country, even if they did not lake any exclusive claims to their patriotism (Hear, hear.) -Rampant Imperialism they depreeeted as much as their friend Mr Pierpoint, who had just treatea them to a pretty severe criticism of it. Sane Imperial- ism, all that was necessary for the defence of our Em- ' pire and our commerce and legitimate prestige, they supported, not from party motives, but from convic- tion ; and with what Lord Rosebery had called this " larger patriotism " they saw their way Co unite a progressive policy at home. (Hear, hear.) There was something very distasteful in making party capital out of patriotism (Hear, hear.) They were quite as good patriots as any of their enoonents. ;Applause.) Just as votes were bought in 1895 by promises of old age pensions, so now a great deal o? mischievous work had been done by throwing dust into the eyes of people by the preaching of what was called patriotism, (Loud applause.) The following received prizes at the hands of Mr Gros- field:-1. 0 Strange, lady's chain; 2, G H Shaw, marble clock; 3, L Auckland, set of bowls: 4. R Wnitfield, travelling bag ; 5, F Rigby. lady's ring ; 6, R Morrow, cruet; 7, C H Hibbert, bedroom clock; 8, H Daintith, tea pot; 9, T Critchley, butter dish; 10. Mr. Crosfield's generosity and virtues were known to all of them, and no words he could add wouli raise him in their estimation. One of the highest testimonies to his character was given during the lee campaign. when Alderman Franoomb asked the electors to give Mr. Crosfielei a good thrashing, and, he added, he could assure them that with his gentlemanly charac- ter and tele sportsmanship he would take the defeat in eood tart, come up smiling, and continue the many generous acts for which he Was noted. They knew Mr. Crestiele's skill in polities, and in golf, and they had had that evening an instance of his skill as a performer on the p ann. He did net know how far he had gone in the garn,) of bevels. Perhaps the game was not such an aristocratic one as golf,but he betieved bowls was a royal game of England. He believed it was a historical fact that Sir Francis Drake was engaged in a game of bole on Plymouth Hoe when the Spanish Armada was in sight. brake said : " W have time to finish the game of bowls and thrash the Seeniards afterwards." (Laughter.) He (Mr Ilibbsrt) hoped that a somewhat similar result might have followed Mr Creafiehi's golf experiences in America and that was when he came to tight the Tories in Warrington he might have been able to boat them. (A Voice: "Next time.") (Hear, hear.) The merabere of the Bowling Club were all pleased to have Mr Crosfield as president. The prizes which be ()Jeered, stimulated the members to become ex- pert in the gams. They could not have a wordiier president and they ought to retain the name of Crosfield which had been a household word in Warrington for three generations. Be trusted that before long Mr. Crosfield might occupy in the hearts of Warrington people generally the same high regard and esteem in which he was held by the members of the club. (Ap- plans ) Mr LOCKER said it was larely owing to Mr Crosfield's generosity that they had had such Aucc,,qsfal seasons. They were improving every year, not only by an in- crease of members but by better bowlers The green was in excellent order, thanks to the services of Mr Lamb, won had left nothing undone to facilitate the pleasure of the bowlers. (Hear, hear). They had also a very good joint secretary in Mr Freeman who had worked hard throughout the season, and to whom much of the success of the club was due. (Hear, hear.) The club was in peeeeseion of an excellent green, situated as it was in the ceetre of the town. But it was necessary to improve the surroandings of the ground and :nake it as weeny a spot as any in Warringeen. Mr. CROSFIE,D, in reply, said he never cams to the club without receiving great courtesy and kindness, and it added to one's pleasure from year to year to occupy such an honourable position as that of 'President. The old associations of his father end others had a certain influence on his mind, and would make it very difficult for him to sever his connection with the place, or refuse to help to carry on the work of Liberalism in the town. (Applause.) It must be very gratifying to them, as it was to him, to see the club going so strong in the matter of billiards and bowls. Mr. Hibbert had referred to the last name 1 game. He remembered the late Richard Ceta den on one occasion remarking to his unele George at Walton Lea, when his uncle gave Mr Cobden a goosl beating, "Oh, Crosfield, what a lot of time you must have wasted at this game." He (the speaker) had ' either spent or wasted a good deal of time at various vines, and he could tell Mr [fibbed that he played at the game of bowls very early in life. He began when he could scarcely toddle across the green by carrying what they called a " footer." (Laughter.) He used to carry it when his father played bowls on e summer evening at Lynam, and that gave him an additional interest in following the fortunes of Warrington clubs, and especially the one at the Liberal Club. He admired a keen competition on a green. and I he liked to see people (wile the game. It was a great pleasure to him to de what he could to further the games of bewls and billiards in connection with that and other clubs. Before he depleted he would like to take advantage of that opportunity of thanking those who fought an uphill battle during the recent election. Councillor TINNION.: he had often thanked before for what he had dune for this club. By his staunch and strenuous support of Liberalism outside of it he was rendering a yet greater and more important service to the Liberal party in the town. (Cheers.) Then Mr Furness was indefatigable, and he was sure they all admired the wee he worked and were most grateful to him for it. (Hear. hear.) Mr Councillor Plumpton—tlie genial Councillor if he mient call him so—yes not here to-night, but he was in evidence all the time of the election, cheerful and imperrurbible whatever the odds against them. (Hear, hear.) What should he say of his election agent? That he wou'd almost sooner lose in working with him, than win with anyone else. He did not believe any candidate in the gineedom had a more pleasant cemnanien and judicious counsellor to work with. The Liberal Party loolchl for great things in the future from this rising and capable men, and he would take it upon hire,to ear they would no-, be disappointed. (Cheers.) He elieuld Ilee to continue the list ; for maey other energetic workers took A prominent nest in the fight where we made so good a show. (Hear, hear.) Beceuse,all thingstconsiderei,they did make ra very good fight of it. (Hear, hear.) In cenclusien, Mr Crosfield referred to the excellent artiste who had contributed to the enjoyment of the evening, and congratulated Mr Pemberton on having brought such musical talent tegether.

THE EXPERIENCES OF A LUNATIC ATTENDANT. Edward Robertson an assistant lunatic attendant, deposed to putting the deceased to bed. Witness was told by Dr. Peacocke that the nurse would bring some medicine. A few minutes afterwards Nurse McCormick came and gave Woods the medicine. Witness made the remark that the deceased was "inclined to be rough." Woods fancied he could see faces through the window and wanted to get up. He tore his shirt and the bedclothes. The Matron tele- phoned for Dr. Braids, and he saw her do so. It was found that the doctor was out. Witness saw Nurse Mc- Cormick (the night nurse), and asked "Is it time to okra that man hie draught ?" The nurse administered it whilst witness held Woods's baud. Woods was very violent until half-past two, when he went to sleep. He supposed the draught had then taken effect. He had previously tied a sheet round the deceased to keep the clothes on him and to cover him. When he awoke the deceased talked but was not violent. Dobson, the head lunatic attendant, came at 8.15 and he called his atten- tion to Whoth's-condition, remarAing nat be wan vary poorly." Do.beon left about half past six to take a re- port to the Matron, and Nurse McCormick took his place at about a quarter-to seven. At ten minutes past seven witness left the man in the bands of the day attendant. Some strength was required to keep the man in bed. Between twelve and one o'clock the man was very rough.
By Mr Hickman : fie did not see deceased have any medicine after the draught,

div.head: WORKHOUSE INMATE'S DEATH AT WARRINGTON. Inquiry by the Local Government Board.
div.p: A WORKHOUSE INMATE'S DEATH AT WARRINGTON. Inquiry by the Local Government Board.
Was Anyone to Blame ?

At the Workhouse, Warrington, on Tuesday, Mr. Jenner Fast, one of the inspectors of the Local Government Board, was engaged the whole of the day inquiring into the circumstances attending the death of an inmate of the Workhouse named Seth Woods, formerly lodging at 35, Wetkin-street. Mr. FuLt was accompanied by Mr. lloorsona, assistant inspector.
The Inspector explained at the outset that no one in particular wasi implicated. It might come nut in the course of the evidence either that no one was to blame or that someone was.

There were present Mrs Clay, and Messrs A J Jolley (chairman of the Board), Clarke, Thornton, Aslscroft, Billin, G Pillin. Hickman. Houeh ton, and Brolks (2uardian 4), J C Sutton (clerk), Sutton (assistant clf-rk), C H Ward (waster), Drs Peacocks and Prraid4, Mrs Ward (matron), and several of the nurses. Dr Adam; was also in attendance. A RELIEVING OFFICERI3 EVIDENCE.

The firs'c. witness called was Mr Basil Shearer assistant relieving officer of the Union. On the 22ncl August he received a certificate from Dr. Adams with reference to Woods, which stated that the man should be placed under restraint at once. He received that about seven o'clock at night. He telephoned to Dr Peacr+cke, the medical officer for that district, and asked him to stay in the surgery till witness came to him in a cab. Efe then sent for a cab and went to Dr Peacocke's, and they journeyed together to3s,Watkin-street,where they found Woods in lodgings. The doctor examined him, and mid that he had to be got ready to be taken to the Workhouse. It was stated that Woods had been very violent during the day, and had tried to get through the window. He was then excited, bat otherwise quiet and respect- ful. The man was put in a cab, and witness got in with him. The doctor rode with the driver. On the way the man asked where he was being taken, and he was toll. He protested, stating that there was inthing the matter with him, and that he could take care of himself. Woods smartly walked up the workhouse steps without assistance, and he was taken through to the lunatic ward. The time was eight orcicick... Woods was given into the charge of the attendant, Robertson. He told the matron that the man was Buff6ring from delirium treyzens. Witness also explained that he was suffer- ing from pneumonia- In answer to the Inspector, witness stated that he described Woods as an alleged lunatic in older give the three days' certificate.
Ii anqwer to kir. Sutton, witness stated that the deceased was 33 years of age, and was employed in coalyard, belonging to Messrs. Pearson and Knowles.
DEL lIDA.EVeg TESTIMONY.

Dr. Adams. surgeon to the workmen of Messrs Pearson and Knowles, said his attention was called to the deceased on the 22nd August, and he ex- amined him and gave the certificate now produced. Witness's partner had seen the deceased previously, and had attended him, He saw the deceased at his Dr Curtis's) request. as Woods had been very vio- lent. Witness found the deceased suffering from r 'ute alcoholism and acute pneumonia. Other par- tic-liars ware given,and the doctor added that it was quite impossible to restrain the man, who was very N ;o1 An t. The delirium was, he thought,mora due to the pneumonia; there were fewer of the alcoholic delusions. Witness, having made arrangements for •vioods's removal, resigned all further charge of the case. By Mr. 9utton : The man was suffering from a severe illness, aggravated by drink.

Dr. Peacocke. district medical officer for the No. 1 dis- t said on the 22n1 August his attention was dzawn ,7he case by Mr Shearer, by a telephonic meisage. Vd.cness went to Woods' lodgings. Deceased was stand- ing in the kitchen half-dressed, and he was in an ex- cited con lition. He felt his pulse, and it seemed fairly co-d and he thought from his condition and from Dr. Adams's certificate, that the sooner he was removed to the Workhouse the better. He made no further examina- tinn. fl e saw the man into the lunatic ward, and saw , n undregged and nut to bed by the lunatic attendant. H `.gain felt his pulse,but made no exhaustive examine- tioL of any kind, as he deemed it unnecessary. He told L;oe attendant that he might expect the deceased to be 1:cou01 during the night, and that he (witness) would send him some medicine from the surgery. He gave the .nan a stimulating draught. Certain instructions were riven to the nurse as to the treatment of the deceased. He blieved the Matron was the first official he saw. He bel(eved he saw her daughter. He told the Matron that the mKn WA'S suffering from pneumonia and delirium tr, -.ens, He could not of his own knowledge state that I , suffering from pneumonia. Subsequently he ,eived a letter from the Mister of the Workhouse.ask- b,g him certain questions. The letter produced was his. 01 the 5-41 S eptemher he wrote a letter in reply to one r6celved from the Master :—"ln reply to the committee, i 3 Seth I,Voods, I beg to reply that! was cognizant of the fact that he was suffering from pneumonia. In answer to the second question, / am almost certain I 'nformed the Matron. Mrs. Ward." He repeated now Ahat he was almost certain he told the Matron about the pneumonia. Be thought it undr.sirable to make a further examination of the deceased', seeing the condition he was in. The treatment he adopted was correct whether the delirum was due to pneumonia or alcoholism. Had he kin-na etacr,ly that the condition of his lungs was as stated by Dr. Adams he should have treated Woods in the same manner.

Bv vie. Sutton: Ha was Dr Beside's deputy, and he thought that the deceased had better see a medical man at once. Be thought it desirable to act on his behalf that night. Be wishei to save Dr Braide a journey to the Workhouse. He felt absolutely certlin as to the directions given by him to the nurss. Mrs. Ward, the Matron, said she remembered the ad- tTiiSSiri of Yools. She saw him in the entrance hall with Dr. Peacock, and Mr. Shearer. Dr. Peacooke said he would take the man to the lunatic ward. She said she must telephone for Dr Bride. but Dr Peacocks said he was taking the case for him. Oa returning Mr Shearer sail it was a Case of delirium tremens and Dr Peacock. added nhernonia. She (Mrs Ward) also tele- phoned to Dr Braide to the effect that the attendant wanted th jacket for the patient, who was worse. Edith Mary Ward, formerly schoolmistress in the house said that she heard Dr Peacocks tell her mother I that 1::13 had given the nurse full instructions for the night. She could not swear that the doc:or said h e had told the nurse to give the medicine every four hours, but it was her strong impression that be did so. Evidence was also given by George Dobson and Henry Thomasson, lunatic attendants. DR.. BRAID AND TElt? CASH. Dr. Braide raid the telephonic message sent on the night of the 22nd was brought to his knowledge about eight o'clock. A second message was received the same evening while he was out. The first mesgage said the man bad been admitt?d suffering from dt?ir it in tremens and pneumonia, and that Dr Peaco;ke had said that he would attend to the case for him. The secoed message reached him absut twenty minutes past ten. It was to the effect that Robertson bad been to the office for leave to restrain the patient, and such leave was not granted to him. Mrs Braid° said that she had asked Mrs Ward whether he (witness) should ring up the Workhouse when he came in and she replied no,she was toe tired and wanted to go to bed. The neat morning, about a quarter past eight, Mr Ward telephoned that the patient sass much worse and gaining in temp,rature. He tGld Mr Ward that he would come as soon as poisi- hie, butt as was afraid he could not get there before ten He left Lie (louse at a quarter to ten, called on one patient, a.ad then went to the Workhouse. Ho proceeded to examine the patient, who was in a very critical condition. He had double pneumonia and the pulse was weak and poor. He prescribed for him, and ordered the diet he was to have, Sze. He then went round the other wards. At about two o'clock he received at his house a message from the Workhouse from Nurse Bray, who told him that the man w.s very much worse. He instructed her to a.k for four ounces of brand,,, to give one ounce to the patient at once, and other clean- titles every three hours. He did not know whether he told the nnrse be would come down. He telephoned for a cab, and waited for it. About ten minutes afterwards the nurse telephoned to say that the man was dead, and be countermanded the order for the cab. On the day of the death,about eight o'clock,he bad to call at the Work- house again, and on that occasion he saw both Mr and Mrs Ward,who.in the course of conversatlon,informed him that Nurse McCormick bad not done her duty in Woods' case the night previous, and that Mr Ward intended to report the matter to the House Committee. On the 24th witness signed the death certificate of Seth Woods. He notified the death to the Local Government Board as occurring within 48 hours after admission. The disease —the pneumonia—was the cause of the delirium. The man had-a slight muttering delirium when witness saw him. To the best of his knowledge he did not fill up any bed card. The entry about the 4oz of brandy was not in his handwriting. His surgery hours were from nine to ten for private and pauper patients. If he bad coma to the Workhouse first h 3 should have arrived there an hour earlier. Be went to a private ease first. Ha was aware that the pauper patients took precedence of his private patients. He recognized that Woods's was a serous ease.

Tno Inspector : If Woos's case bad received from everyone the greatest care and attention possible, could that have made any difference in the result? Witness : I don't think there 'vas a chance of his re- cover, juiging from the conditkn he was in when I saw him.
Tn 3 Inipeotor : I am nnt savinz he did not rec,ive evPry MO and attention. I am putting it nypothoti— ealiv.
Witness, continuing, said it was undoubtedly a case of pnennaonia.

By the Chairman: He remembered attending a meet- inE,. of the House Committee on the 31st Aimust. He did no"; say the man was no: suffering from del;mung tremens. He expressed the opinion that the delirium proceeded mainly from the pneumonia. He also said that 80 per cent of case; of double pneumonia terminated fatally. He said he was not in a position to judv what the treatment ought to have been the night before.

_ By the In3pec`or : He could not express an opinion as to whether Woods ought to have had frequent nurs- ing atter:dance during the nigh, only having his condi- tion at eleven o'clock the following morning to judge by. The man was able to walk about the night before. As a ma-tel of fact, he knew that in two cases of equal urgency thl pauper patient had to be treated first. The Clerk to the Guardians produced the book of the porter containing entries relating to Auguit 22nd .nd 23rd.
Mr. Shear.r re-called, said that durinz the fjni he was fit tho Wolchluss he clic] not hear anything said about m7dieine being administered every four hours during the night.
THE INSPECTOR THANKED.

At the closl of the inquiry, lit:: AT Jolley thanked the Inspector for his patience in hearing the evidence of the witnesses, and said that the only object he and his fellow-members of the Bard had in view was to get at the truth of the matter, and to see that the nursing was well and carefully done.

Toe Inspector briefly returned thsnks, and intimated that he had rece;vrd f;•reat assistance from Mr. Jolley. The Board would in eup comic receive a communication from the Local Gc. v,e;'--ircent Board. OLD FALSE TEETH BOUGHT.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Rugby Football.
[By " Ovalist."'

I am dis zusted with Warrington. Saturday's dis- play against Runcorn was disgraceful, and instead of the hoped for victory another defeat was chronicled. For fourteen years have the " Linnets" trounced the Warringtmn men and the chance of turning the tables seems as far off as ever. It ought to have been done on Saturday,and would have been done had the Warrin2ton men shaped anything like a Lancashire Senior Com- petition club, for the home team was in sore straits, being minus Houghton, T Warder, J Butterworth and C Butterworth, all of the back division and a quartette it would be diffi- cult to beat. On the other hand Warrington were fully represented, in fact an effort had been made to improve upon the regular team by substituting Dickin- son for Lawless at centre, but the change did not work satisfactorily. The game was evenly contested, and at times it looked as if Warrington would win but the a,bso• lute lack of backbone in the team caused them to fall a couple of points short of the Runcorn score.

To say that the supporters of the" Wirepullers" were disappointei does not half express their feelings. They were enraged as welt as disappointed. Here was the loveliest of chances for smitiag the" Linnets " hip and thigh thrown away by a display of football worse thaw ustaal even for Warrington. Had they only playe d up to their own standard they would have won, but bo ! for Runcorn's benefit they played about as badly as a team could. No wonder the faeeo of Warringtonians wore a dejected and angry look when the match was over. I should not like to be a committeeman just at present. "Save me from my friends," as well as enemies, must be what they are thinking.

On arrival at the port, prospects of victory seemei brighter than ever for it was found that the home team's skipper; the veteran Houghton, was unable to turn out as expected and Jolley had to fill his place. Thus disor- ganised the Runcorn men entered the arena, an i ob- tained what help there was from winning the toss. warrington begun splendidly,smart work all round pen- ning the bomestz.rs in, and befote five minutes had elapsed Fish dodged his way over the goal line at the corner, and Warrington were a try ahead. Runcorn rallied at this, and showed their fine spirit by the way they forced Warrington back and made repeated efforts to get through. The Warrin.gtort line had narrow escapes galore but appeared likely te stand the strain until Burgess hurt his knee and left the field for ten minutes. During this brief interval the homesters got their noses in front. Jolley k;clc-..d a fine goal from a mark, and Faulkner blufLd his opponents cleverly and scored near the posts. The success in- spired the homesters and shocking play by the Warring- ton backs prevented them clearing out the invaders. It is long since I saw such repeated mulling and funky play, and the result was that Runcorn got another try, Richardson being the silorer from a pack near the line. At the interval the home team held the comfortable lead of 8 points to 3 points.

The second half was little better from a Warrington point of view, no advantage being taken of the wind, slope, and sun to make a desperate effort. Runcorn won easily forward and maintained a menacing attitude most of the time. It was only Hallam's expert defence and Fish's frequent inroads that enabled Warrington to make any show at O. The rest of the team was helpless, Bate alone doing himself justice. Runcorn got two more points. Richardson dropping a goal, and then Warrington's lamp made one despairing flicker before popping out. Bate t WiC9 tried to get Fish in and the second time the County three-quarter got a yard start of hic opponents, sprinted for the line like a deernound, clEared Jolley with a bound., and scored as fine a try as anybody nee.d wish to see. He was also successful with the goal-kick, and his brilliant effort WAS cheered to the echo. Warringtora tried hard to wipe off the remaining two points, but time was short and the " Linnets" easily held their own to the end, winning very creditably by 10 points to 8 points.

Perhaps Runcorn were a little fortunate in obtaining five points during the absence of Burgess,and a dropped goal which it is alleged one of the Warrington forwards nullified by touching the ball, but ab any rate there is no excuse fo: Warrington in not winning. They had opportunities enough, and even had the backs defended as reliably as they can at times, Warrington would have won. It was bad defence which allowed Runcorn to score both tries, whereats there was absolutely no stop- ping Fish on either occasion.To e•lsherv.-ond miss catch after catch and Bate and Dickinson do likewis, was enough to make angels weep. What has come over Warrington's once sound centre I can't imagine. He has lost all the steadines,a, all the dash, and all the skill that he once possessed—let us hope only temporarily. On form, however, it is a fact that he is not fit for his place. But there is no better substitute. Dickinson was, aa I expected, too incaperienced and youthful to cope with the Runcorn men and will have to train on in the" A" team. Lawless is not much better, and altogether Warrington are worse off at cen- tre than they have been for years, and it is time they realised the fact. In fact there are only three class men in the team, Fish, Hallam, and' Bate, and the lat er is not the Bate of yore. The forwards are like- wise too light to hold their own in every match. They were hopelessly beaten by the Runcorn eight. Warrington were thoroughly shown sip on Saturday, and the conclusion was obvious that they are little superior to a second division team.

For some time efforts—of a kind—have been in pro- gress to obtain new blood. Men have been away every meek with authority to soap up any bargain in football 119 sh that presents itself, but so far they have signally I failed. And when were they successful at any time in the past? Never. The Warrington club does not boast of a single player of repute who has been brought from afar, and yet representatives of the!club have been "try- ing" for years. Surely they can do better, It is no good saying men cannot be got, they can and must be. Rochdale Hornets can get them andwhy not Warrington? If the slightest improvement on past records is going to be made this season they will have to be got promptly. A ten pound note will not do it—a lmodred pounds might—and it is worth Warrington's while to put this suna down and secure a really class centre. Having got this off my mind I feel rather better. It has been grow- ing there for weeks..

On their respective Rides on Saturday Fish and Hallam were the pick of Warrington, and Faulkner and Jolley the same for Runcorn. Jones, Richardson, and Welker also performing excellently for the homesters. There is little more to be said excvt to ask what would have been the result had Runc)rn turned out with a full team. Oi to put it another way. how Warrington would have shaped with the best men in the back divi- sion on the injured list P They would not have won. would they P Well, Runcorn did under similar circum- stances. That about shoTs the disparity between the two teams this season.
